Haaland averaged 2.0 points and 1.1 rebounds in 10 appearances last season, making his lone start on Senior Day against Portland on Feb. 25. Haaland scored a career-high 10 points with four rebounds in 11 minutes against Pepperdine on Jan. 21, going 4 of 4 from the field and 2 of 2 from the free throw line.

The 6-foot-9 forward played two seasons at Allan Hancock College in California before transferring to Gonzaga in 2024. At Lakeland High, he earned All-4A Inland Empire League honors as a junior and senior, helping the Hawks advance to the 4A state tournament in 2021.

Haaland’s father, Dale, played two seasons at Gonzaga from 1985-87 and his mother, Robyn Benson, is a former Zags volleyball player.

Gonzaga.title: Ivy League opponent Cornell visiting Gonzaga for New Year's Eve nonconference matchup
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga will face an Ivy League opponent on New Year’s Eve before turning the page on its nonconference schedule and diving into Pac-12 Conference play.

Mark Few’s program will host Cornell on Dec. 31, according to a report on Friday from Bracketeer.com’s Rocco Miller. A tipoff time and television details will be announced at a later date.

The New Year’s Eve matchup technically won’t mark the end of GU’s nonconference schedule – the Zags will travel to Detroit on Feb. 20 to play Duke – but is expected to be the final nonleague game before Few’s team opens Pac-12 play in January.

The Cornell matchup becomes the fourth known home nonconference game for Gonzaga, which will also host New Mexico State (Nov. 7), Montana State (Nov. 17) and NAIA Eastern Oregon (Dec. 2). LSU is also visiting Spokane for a Nov. 14 matchup at Numerica Veterans Arena.

This will be the first-ever meeting between Gonzaga and Cornell and signifies just the second matchup between the Zags and an opponent from the Ivy League. Yale visited Spokane on two occasions, traveling to Numerica Veterans Arena in 1992 before returning to play at McCarthey Athletic Center in 2023.

Cornell placed fourth in the Ivy League standings last season, finishing with an overall record of 15-13 and conference mark of 8-6.

Third-year coach Jon Jaques, a former Cornell captain from 2006-10, is replacing each of his three double-digit scorers from a year ago, including guards Cooper Noard (18.2 points per game) and Jake Fiegen (17.1 ppg). The team’s top returner is starting point guard Jacob Beccles, who averaged 7.7 points, 3.1 assists and 2.5 rebounds.

Gonzaga’s nonconference schedule still hasn’t been finalized, but as of now the Cornell matchup is the team’s only game between a Dec. 19 showdown with Michigan State in Palm Springs and the end of the calendar year.

Gonzaga.title: How Gonzaga's offseason evolved into a roster-building roller coaster: 'Like nothing we've ever seen'
Gonzaga.summary:
The catalogue of words Mark Few could use to describe Gonzaga’s offseason is too long to run through, but the newly enshrined Hall of Fame coach landed on some appropriate terms during a breakdown of the five-ish months that have elapsed since his team exited the NCAA Tournament with a Round of 32 loss to Texas.

First, there was “frustrating,” followed by “not usual” and finally “crazy.”

“Like nothing we’ve ever seen and it’s been frustrating, but it’s just different in this day and age,” Few said last weekend during a media session at Mohegan Sun Casino in Uncasville, Connecticut, one day before he was enshrined into the Naismith Hall of Fame. “It’s been not usual, but like we just got done talking about, you have to adapt.”

“Turbulent” might be another term to characterize the roster-building roller coaster Few and his coaching staff have navigated since the early stages of April.

Just 44 days out from Kraziness in the Kennel, Gonzaga has eight scholarship players officially signed to its 2026-27 roster with two more walk-ons. In other words, if the Zags held their annual Kraziness showcase tomorrow, they’d have exactly the number of bodies required to run through a traditional 5-on-5 intrasquad scrimmage, but no more than that.

A full roster is still expected the time Gonzaga opens the season on Nov. 2 against Purdue for a potential top-25 showdown in Las Vegas, but it could hinge on a number of things well outside of Few’s control – something that’s become a primary source of angst for the new Hall of Famer and coaching peers around the country the last handful of months as they try to finalize their teams before the fall semester starts.

The issues Gonzaga faces now are partially a byproduct of unforeseen developments that came earlier in the offseason. When former signee Jack Kayil unexpectedly kept his name in the NBA Draft on May 13, most quality transfer portal options at his position had already committed to play elsewhere, limiting Gonzaga’s replacement options. (Kayil was selected No. 39 overall by the New York Knicks, but the combo guard will be stashed in Europe after signing a five-year extension with German club Alba Berlin).

The transfer portal was bone-dry when starting point guard Mario Saint-Supery abruptly left Gonzaga’s program, catching fans and Few’s coaching staff completely off guard on July 11 when he signed a four-year, seven-figure contract with Spanish ACB club Valencia.

Gonzaga had a contingency plan in place, but even that has come with complications.

On June 26, the Zags landed a commitment from French guard Nathan De Sousa, a 23-year-old professional who’s spent the last five seasons with Cholet of LNB Elite. De Sousa would’ve been a top-notch backup to Saint-Supery and could prove to be more than serviceable as a starter in the new Pac-12 Conference, but both he and Gonzaga forward commit Izan Almansa – a 6-foot-10 forward who played last season at Real Madrid – are still waiting on the NCAA to approve eligibility waivers.

In an attempt to prohibit highly compensated European pros from entering college basketball, the sport’s governing body indicated earlier this summer it would not clear any player who was paid above “actual and necessary expenses.”

“We’ve had several of the European kids that the NCAA’s kind of acted like they’re going to change how they interpret these and they didn’t even do it midstream, they did it when you’re already through your recruiting cycle, which has just been crazy,” Few said. “We voiced our concerns, all of us coaches have to them. We don’t know what’s going to happen with how they rule Europeans, even though they were letting everyone in last year. Now the five-year thing has happened…”

Ah yes, the five-year thing.

Gonzaga’s second contingency plan has transformed into a late-summer headache for coaches and players around the country. It stems from the NCAA’s decision in late June to adopt age-based eligibility rules, allowing athletes to play five seasons over five years.

The new rules weren’t intended to grandfather in seniors who completed their eligibility in 2025-26, but the NCAA’s timing gave a large crowd of fifth-year hopefuls a long enough runway to challenge the regulatory body in court with hopes of securing another season.

“Listen, I think if the courts are going to rule them eligible and they’re eligible, I don’t know why anybody would ever say anything about them,” Few said. “I think many people have spoke about how that particular class is the only one that hasn’t had this. Moving forward they’re going to have it and behind them was COVID. It’s one class so you’re like, ‘yeah they’re right.’ ”

Now, less than two months out from preseason exhibition games, programs like Gonzaga have made late-summer additions fill holes at certain positions and generally erase any lingering uncertainty around their rosters.

The result? More uncertainty.

Gonzaga picked up two quick commitments, one from 5-10 Dayton point guard Javon Bennett, who was ruled eligible after prevailing in an Ohio lawsuit, and another from 6-10 Florida State wing Chauncey Wiggins, who won a similar case in his home state of Georgia.

Neither have signed financial aid agreements with Gonzaga, and there’s some apprehension around Bennett’s situation after the NCAA was granted a motion to stay the Ohio case on Monday, potentially reversing the guard’s eligibility. Bennett is still protected by the federal Wisne vs. NCAA injunction approved earlier this month in Colorado, but the guard could encounter another hurdle if the NCAA is also granted a stay in that case.

“It’s definitely a crazy time in college basketball,” Bennett said. “For me, when I heard I was left out of that 5-in-5 window, I was definitely devastated. I think if you’re going to give players after us a chance, I don’t see why we wouldn’t be able to get a chance. I think it’s fair for us to appeal to that situation and like I said, I think kids that have somewhere to play will be able to benefit from the 5-in-5.”

Wiggins, who could figure into Gonzaga’s starting lineup at the small forward spot after averaging 13.3 pints and making 38.7% of his 3-pointers last season, is on solid ground for the time being as someone protected by both the Georgia and Colorado federal lawsuits.

“I do think the NCAA should’ve grandfathered us in,” Wiggins said. “The way I see it is, when my class got into college we played against fifth-year and sixth-years. Then when we’re about to leave college, you’re telling me you’re going to give everybody after us five years. And some of us, I think like me still fit that age. The age requirement they were talking about, I fit that. Some of us in the 2022 class fit that, so I think the NCAA personally should’ve gave us another year.

“College sports is college sports, it’s got some chaos right now. I do think they will appeal – I don’t really know, but I think they might appeal the Colorado one because that was for everybody and it came out of the blue.”

Coaches who’ve already finalized their rosters, or refuse to dip into the 5-in-5 pool out of principle, have been critical of peers relying on fifth-year players to improve their teams.

“At some point, you’ve got to care about the sport,” UConn’s Dan Hurley said. “Especially if the sport has given you a lot. Doing things to hurt the sport so that you can win a little bit more, you’ve got to look in the mirror a little on that.”

Few, who’s been on numerous coaching and college basketball committees throughout his 28-year tenure at Gonzaga, was one of the coaches imploring the NCAA to wait on announcing new 5-in-5 eligibility rules, anticipating the chaos that’s ensued over the last two months.

“Behind the scenes, some of us coaches told the NCAA over and over again,” Few said. “If they waited longer to announce this, they probably wouldn’t have this issue. So I don’t know why anybody would not be open to it. Maybe you don’t need it, but if you do … these are good guys. The kids we’re recruiting graduated from college, they’re going to our grad school and they’re great people, great assets to our program. I don’t know why you wouldn’t do that.”

In this fluid college basketball climate, it could be a matter of days, weeks or months until Gonzaga is able to call its roster complete. It’s not unfamiliar territory for a program that waited on a judge’s decision at the 11th hour last season to learn if transfer wing Tyon Grant-Foster would be eligible to play.

The Zags ostensibly received positive news on Thursday, when Real Madrid penned a farewell letter to Almansa, suggesting the forward is one step closer to making it official with Few’s program.

For now, a frustrating, crazy and unusual Gonzaga offseason will bleed into the final days of August.

Gonzaga.title: Montana State program coming off strong Big Sky season set to visit Gonzaga on Nov. 17
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga hasn’t released its final nonconference schedule, but anyone willing to do some digging can probably discover a few of the missing pieces.

For example, a quick internet search of Montana State’s schedule would’ve led someone to the third known home game of Gonzaga’s 2026-27 nonleague slate.

According to Montana State’s athletics website, the Bobcats are scheduled to visit Gonzaga on Nov. 17, one week before Mark Few’s program takes on the 16-team Players Era Festival in Las Vegas.

A tipoff time and television broadcast details will be announced at a later date.

SB Nation’s Gonzaga website, Slipper Still Fits, identified the matchup with Montana State hours after The Spokesman-Review discovered another home game against NAIA Eastern Oregon, thanks to an updated schedule on the Mountaineers’ site.

With the additions of Montana State and Eastern Oregon, the Zags now have 12 known dates on their nonconference schedule, not including a potential championship matchup at the Players Era event on Nov. 28. Gonzaga will play at least four nonleague games in Spokane and won’t have to leave town between a Nov. 2 opener against Purdue at T-Mobile Arena in Vegas and the team’s return to Sin City on Nov. 24 for Players Era.

There have been 49 previous meetings between Gonzaga and Montana State, but none since 1997, with a majority of the prior matchups occurring while both programs were part of the Big Sky Conference. The Zags have a 27-22 advantage in the all-time series and have prevailed in seven of the last nine meetings.

Under the guidance of fourth-year coach Matt Logie, who earned a four-year contract extension on Wednesday, the Bobcats have won exactly 50% of their games, going 18-14 last season, 15-18 in 2024-25 and 17-18 in 2023-24 for a total record of 50-50. Montana State earned an automatic NCAA Tournament berth during Logie’s first season, marking the program’s third straight trip to March Madness. The Bobcats went each of the two previous years under former coach Danny Sprinkle, who’s now at Washington.

Montana State loses its top three scorers from a team that finished second in the Big Sky with a 12-6 record before losing to Idaho in the second round of the conference tournament.

The Bobcats have to replace more than 31 points per game from their starting lineup, but they do return their fourth, fifth and sixth-leading scorers, including forward Christian King, a Kirkland native and Seattle Prep graduate who averaged 12.6 points and 4.5 rebounds last season.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga scheduled to host familiar NAIA opponent for nonconference game on Dec. 2
Gonzaga.summary:
Another home date has been added to Gonzaga’s nonconference calendar.

Eastern Oregon, an NAIA program that has frequented McCarthey Athletic Center over the years, is returning to Spokane for a nonleague game on Dec. 2, according to the Mountaineers’ schedule.

The matchup will figure into Gonzaga’s overall record but count as an exhibition for Eastern Oregon, which competes in the Cascade Collegiate Conference. It becomes the second known home game on the Zags’ nonconference schedule and third known game in Spokane, joining the Nov. 7 home opener against New Mexico State and Nov. 14 matchup against LSU at Numerica Veterans Arena.

The Mountaineers have made three recent trips to the Kennel under sixth-year coach Matt Kemp, visiting on Oct. 31, 2021, for a matchup that counted as an exhibition for both teams. The Zags had six players reach double figures en route to a 115-62 victory.

Each of Eastern Oregon’s last two visits were exhibition contests for the Mountaineers that factored into Gonzaga’s regular-season schedule. That included a 120-42 victory for Gonzaga on Dec. 28, 2022, that signified the largest margin of victory in program history. Drew Timme led seven double-digit scorers with 18 points in 18 minutes.

Gonzaga cleared the century mark for the third time in as many meetings the next season, winning 123-57 on Nov. 14, 2023. Graham Ike was one of three 20-point scorers for GU, leading the game with 25 points and 11 rebounds in just 18 minutes. Braden Huff, the only player from that game who will suit up against EOU this fall, had 23 points for the Zags.

Second-year Gonzaga graduate assistant Que Johnson was on Kemp’s staff at EOU as a top assistant coach for each of the last three meetings between the schools. There are a pair of connections to the Inland Northwest on the Mountaineers’ 2026-27 roster, including former Coeur d’Alene High standout Logan Orchard and Caleb Schroeder, a Post Falls native who played at Genesis Prep.

The Dec. 2 game will either come four or five days after GU’s finishes up at the Players Era in Las Vegas. The Zags will either close the 16-team tournament on Nov. 27 or 28, depending on if they qualify for the championship game.

Three days after the EOU matchup, Gonzaga will travel to play UCLA in a neutral-site, nonconference game at the Honda Center in Anaheim, California.

Washington State.title: How can WSU get its running backs more involved in its offense?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Think back to January, when Washington State coach Kirby Moore pulled off what was seen at the time as a monumental move, putting together a three-man running back room that figured to gash opponents this fall.

Kirby Vorhees, last year’s starter, was planning on entering the transfer portal but decided to return to WSU the night before it opened. Tailback Maxwell Woods also returned to the team. And fellow running back Leo Pulalasi entered the portal, only to reverse course and also sign a new NIL revenue-sharing deal with the Cougars.

Especially under a head coach like Moore, whose best offenses at Missouri involved a productive ground attack, it seemed like the Cougs had struck gold with the return of their top three running backs.

Now let’s fast forward to this last week of September, after WSU’s 1-3 start to the season, the record the Cougars were expected to open the season with. It’s one thing that the Cougs’ offense has struggled in most of these outings. It’s another that one of the bigger culprits is their ground attack, or lack thereof, which has hampered what Moore and offensive coordinator Matt Miller had planned for quarterback Caden Pinnick’s offense.

WSU deserves credit for gashing FCS Duquesne for 316 rushing yards earlier this month, especially because Woods and Vorhees each cleared the 100-yard mark, but it’s also true that the Cougars did that against one of the FCS ranks’ worst defenses. What’s likely more informative is how they’ve fared against FBS competition, even if there’s been something of a talent gap in those games.

In a loss to Washington, WSU’s running back trio combined for 38 yards. In a setback to Kansas State, those three combined for 74. And on Saturday in a defeat to Arizona, they tallied just 59 yards between them. That adds up to 171 yards, which is 57 yards per game – not exactly eyebrow-raising in the way Moore was hoping for ahead of the season.

That forces Moore and Miller to find a way to get them more involved, to find ways to increase their production. How can they do that? Perhaps one way involves getting them more targets in the passing game, which they haven’t enjoyed much so far.

“We gotta find ways to get them matched up,” Moore said. “They make it tough, Arizona does, with how much they pressure because you are worried about the quarterback being hot at times, and you wanna make sure you’re protecting him as much as you can. And then we gotta stay on the field. That’s the best way to get the backs more touches, right? We gotta convert on third downs. The four drives there in the third quarter, we had three punts and a turnover. That’s not good enough.”

Moore had a point. In Saturday’s third quarter, the Cougars punted on three drives and lost a fumble on another, which happened when Pinnick was trying to escape pressure and attempted to throw the ball away while getting dragged down. That was Pinnick’s fifth turnover of the season and WSU’s seventh as a team.

Perhaps more to the point, WSU went 0-for-7 on third down in the second half. That didn’t just take away chances for the Cougars to score. It also removed opportunities for WSU’s tailbacks to involve themselves in the offense, which in turn could have opened up things for Pinnick and Co. Many of WSU’s problems on offense this season have run together, creating an amalgamation of issues. This is no different.

Consider this stat: This season, WSU running backs have been targeted as receivers a combined 22 times. They’ve hauled in receptions on 14. That comes out to a completion percentage of 64, a few ticks up from Pinnick’s 61% overall completion rate . That seems to suggest the Cougars could do well to incorporate more of that in their offense.

WSU gets a chance to prove it on Saturday with a home matchup against Fresno State, which figures to provide more chances to do so than the Power 4 teams that the Cougars’ offense has struggled against.

Washington State.title: WSU set to host Fresno State to kick off competition in rebuilt Pac-12 | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here ’s a first look at Washington State’s home game against Fresno State on Saturday afternoon.

What is it?

To kick off competition in the rebuilt Pac-12, WSU hosts Fresno State, looking to turn around a 1-3 start to the season. In the teams’ first meeting in Pullman since 1994, WSU coach Kirby Moore squares off against the program that gave him his first FBS coaching gig – he worked as the Bulldogs’ receivers coach/offensive coordinator from 2017-22.

In the Cougars’ third straight home game, it’s possible that tight end Trey Leckner makes his season debut after missing the season’s first four games with a foot injury.

Where is it?

Gesa Field at Martin Stadium in Pullman.

When is it?

Kickoff is set for 6:30 p.m.

Where can I watch it?

USA Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored?

As of Monday afternoon, WSU was around a 21/2-point favorite in most sportsbooks.

How did the Cougars fare last week?

In a 34-24 loss to Arizona, WSU took an early lead thanks to one touchdown from QB Caden Pinnick and a pick-six from safety Jackquintin Bal, but Arizona wasted no time leveling the game and won the second half, 20-7. The Cougars drew within one score late on a long touchdown pass from Pinnick to receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, but that’s as close as they came, falling to 1-3 to open Moore’s debut season.

Pinnick completed 24 of 41 passes for 241 yards, two total touchdowns and two turnovers, one interception and one fumble. He’s now lost five turnovers this season, and the Cougars are up to seven as a whole, good for a total turnover margin of minus-4, which is tied for No. 119 nationally. It’s been a key reason behind some of the struggles of offensive coordinator Matt Miller’s group.

The Cougars played an OK game on defense, but they couldn’t slow down Wildcat QB Noah Fifita, who went 22-for-36 passing for 297 yards, four touchdowns and one interception. WSU also couldn’t limit receiver Tre Spivey, who hauled in seven catches for 129 yards and two touchdowns.

Four Cougar defenders played at least 60 snaps, led by cornerback Khamari Terrell with 72, perhaps opening a window into some of the reasons why WSU’s defense wore down in that game: Its best players were on the field too long.

“It adds up in fact that you’re going against a really good quarterback,” Moore said, “and we were very aggressive on defense, and you saw that in the first half. Over time, he’s gonna make some plays. He’s gonna create some passes downfield, and they had the quick drive right there, and just keeping our guys fresh because the coverage and the front, and it’s all gotta work together. If the front is tired and we’re not getting the rush that we want to, well, that’s affecting the back end. That’s what we gotta get solved there in the third quarter, and it really starts playing complementary football.”

In the third quarter, WSU slogged through some listless football, putting up several forgettable numbers: zero points, 149 total yards, 44 rushing yards, two three-and-outs, four punts and three sacks taken, giving Pinnick 10 sacks taken on the season. That opened the door for Arizona to turn a three-point deficit into a four-point lead, cushioning two more scoring drives in the fourth frame.

In the end, it added up to more question marks for WSU’s offense (two turnovers) and its special teams units, which had one field goal blocked and gave up a 39-yard punt return. The Cougars have now had two field goals blocked and given up two long punt returns, including a 62-yarder against Kansas State in Week 2.

The only bright spot on WSU’s special teams group has been punter Max Dean, who battled migraines in Saturday’s game to record five punts for 200 total yards, an average of 40 yards. He’s now averaging 45.2 yards per punt, which ranks No. 14 in the country.

Scouting Fresno State …

The Bulldogs, off to a 3-1 start to the season, are led by second-year head coach Matt Entz and quarterback Jayden Mandal. They began the year with a 39-0 road loss to USC before bouncing back with three straight wins: 49-3 over Sacramento State, 26-10 over San Jose State and 38-24 over Rice, the last of which unfolded last weekend.

Fresno State, which ranks No. 6 in the country with a turnover margin of plus-7, have the Pac-12’s best defense so far. The Bulldogs are allowing just 19 points per game, which ranks at the top in the conference, and star cornerback Simeon Harris has already collected three interceptions. As a team, Fresno State has also recovered three fumbles, tied for the conference lead.

The Bulldogs have also registered nine sacks, second in the conference, including two from linebacker Titus Khajavi and one apiece from six different players. Their Pro Football Focus pass rush grade of 65.3 ranks third in the Pac-12.

“That’s gonna be really important,” Moore said, “to make sure we take care of the football.”

On offense, Mandal has completed 67 of 104 passes (64%) for 789 yards, six touchdowns and one interception. His top target has been senior receiver Josiah Freeman – who was in his true freshman redshirt season in 2022, Moore’s final year at Fresno State – has totaled 18 catches for 261 yards and two touchdowns.

“The receiver was there when I was there. He was a really good, athletic player,” Moore said. “You see him show up on third downs and a lot of different situations.”

But a lot of the Bulldogs’ offense has also come from veteran running back Rayshon Luke, the Pac-12 Offensive Player of the Week. In Fresno State’s win over Rice, he tallied a game and career-high 167 yards with one touchdown on just 11 carries, giving him 240 rushing yards total on the season. He’s also averaging 6.7 yards per carry, which ranks third in the Pac-12.

What happened last time?

WSU and Fresno State’s last meeting came in 2024, when the Cougars eked out a 25-17 road win in Fresno. The Cougars got a key pick-six in the fourth quarter from cornerback Ethan O’Connor, who went on to transfer to Miami over the offseason.

Washington State.title: WSU TE Trey Leckner to be gametime decision against Fresno State, plus other injury updates and notes
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State tight end Trey Leckner is on track to return earlier than anybody quite expected.

That’s the word from coach Kirby Moore, who said Monday that Leckner will be a game-time decision Saturday evening against Fresno State, adding that he “will be back full -go this week in practice.”

A likely starter if he were healthy, Leckner suffered a foot injury over the summer. At the beginning of the season, Moore said Leckner was expected to miss the first half of the season, which would have put his return a few more weeks away. But it appears Leckner has made quicker progress than anticipated.

Whenever he returns, Leckner figures to provide a nice boost to the Cougars’ offense, which is still finding its footing amid the team’s 1-3 start to the season. Leckner is the team’s best pass-catching tight end, which could help unlock a WSU offense that has lost seven total turnovers.

In Leckner’s absence, WSU’s starting tight end has been UCLA transfer Jack Pedersen, who has caught five passes for 20 yards and one touchdown, which came against FCS Duquesne.

“We wanna be able to utilize both those guys. Obviously, try and get our best players on the field on offense,” Moore said. “That’ll probably be determined how (Leckner) looks today, Tuesday, Wednesday with the big work days. But I think he’s really progressed from the previous week, last week, and so he’s definitely shown that in the past, and we’re excited to get him out there.”

A redshirt junior from Snohomish, Leckner started nine of 13 games last season, catching 24 passes for 186 yards and three touchdowns, which tied for the third-most by a tight end in WSU single-season history. In 2024, he played in 12 games (two as a starter), reeling in three passes for 56 yards and one score.

Tucker remains questionable

Starting cornerback Jalil Tucker remains “game-to-game, day-to-day,” Moore said. Tucker has now missed three straight games after sustaining an injury in the Sept. 6 Apple Cup. A transfer from Oregon State, Tucker dressed and warmed up for each of the Cougars’ past two games, but he hasn’t been able to play.

In Tucker’s absence, WSU has tried a couple different approaches. Against Kansas State, the Cougars went with redshirt senior Kai Rapolla, who had a forgettable game, missing two tackles and allowing three catches on four targets. Against Duquesne and Arizona, they moved nickelback Jamarey Smith to cornerback and brought safety Jackquintin Bal off the bench, the latter of which turned out to be a great decision from WSU – Bal returned an interception 25 yards for a touchdown.

If Tucker can’t play Saturday against Fresno State, look for coaches to go with the same approach. They might even give more snaps to Bal, who played a career-high 67 snaps last weekend against Arizona, earning an expanded role in defensive coordinator Trent Bray’s unit. He also recorded nine tackles against Arizona, tops on the team and also Bal’s career-best.

“Just doing my 1/11th, trying to be myself and just try to be the best person I can be in my position,” Bal said after the Arizona game, “no matter if it’s boundary safety, field safety, just doing my part.”

Extra points• Moore seemed to stand by his decision to let 40 seconds tick off the clock at the end of Saturday’s first half against Arizona, when the Cougars had first-and-10 from the Wildcats’ 12-yard line. WSU got a field goal, but Moore explained that he didn’t want to give the ball back to Arizona QB Noah Fifita and his explosive offense.

“Whether we scored or we kicked a field goal too early, giving the ball back to that quarterback,” Moore said, “I did not think was in our best interest before the half.”

• How can the Cougars generate more explosive plays, which Moore has often expressed a need for, when those are the times QB Caden Pinnick has lost turnovers? Moore said this: “It’s definitely a balance. It’s dialogue during the week. If something’s there, if it’s not there, self-preservation, making sure we’re playing the next play. Every play has a life of its own, and we had some of that come up on Saturday.”

Washington State.title: Boise State stands alone after stellar September; still wait-and-see for WSU | Pac-12 power rankings
Washington State.summary:
The Pac-12 football power rankings are published each Sunday on the Hotline and consider both the latest results and seasonlong performance. Call it an objectively subjective look at the state of the conference. If you’re unhappy with the order, email us at the address below … or play better. For comparative purposes, we have included the placement of each team in last week’s rankings.

Boise State was the most important addition when the flattened, desperate Pac-12 reclaimed its future by adding five schools from the Mountain West in September 2024.

Two years and two weeks later, the Broncos are carrying the banner for the rebuilt conference regionally, domestically, internationally and cosmically.

They have emerged from September as the frontrunner for the College Football Playoff berth allocated to the top team in the Group of Six following the close loss to Oregon and convincing victories over Memphis and Western Michigan – two teams that also hold designs on the CFP.

The Broncos are the only team ranked in the AP Top 25 poll this week (No. 22) from outside the power conferences.

They are the top Group of Six team, by a wide margin, in both the Sagarin computer rankings and ESPN’s Football Power Index.

And critically, the Broncos (3-1) have acquired enough resume equity that they can afford one loss in conference play and remain on track for the CFP – assuming, of course, that it’s the right loss: well played, close and to a quality opponent.

Key point: The playoff berth awaiting the top-ranked team in the Group of Six is not reserved for a conference champion; it goes to the best team from the collection of 70.

If the Broncos run the table in the Pac-12 and are 12-1 on CFP selection day (Dec. 6), they’re in.

(That was exactly the same resume they produced in 2024, and it delivered a No. 9 ranking in the selection committee’s final analysis).

If they are 11-2, with that strong nonconference resume and a single loss somewhere within the Pac-12, they would remain well positioned.

At that point, the Broncos would be compared to the zero-, one- or two-loss teams from the American, Mountain West, Sun Belt, MAC and Conference USA.

Their victories over Memphis and Western Michigan – and the narrow loss in Eugene – might be decisive in a resume showdown.

If those teams fare well in their respective leagues, and if Oregon finishes near the top of the Big Ten, the Broncos would compare favorably thanks to an indisputably impressive September.

To the power rankings …

1. Boise State (3-1)

Result: won at Western Michigan 32-7

Next up: vs. Utah State (4:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: The Broncos are averaging 237 yards per game rushing and 204 passing. If you’re curious, they averaged 240 and 226, respectively, two years ago during the playoff drive. Put another way: 51.5% of their total yards were on the ground in 2024 with Ashton Jeanty while 53.7% are on the ground this year with Dylan Riley. (Last week: 1)

2. Oregon State (2-2)

Result: won at UTEP 33-7

Next up: at Colorado State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: As far as the Hotline is concerned, it’s a three-team race for the Pac-12 title, and Oregon State is one of those teams. Which is much more a credit to the Beavers than an indictment on the conference despite the low expectations for OSU (both here and elsewhere). (Last week: 2)

3. Fresno State (3-1)

Result: beat Rice 38-24

Next up: at Washington State (6:30 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: Slow starters, fast finishers: The Bulldogs outscored San Jose State 20-7 in the second half in a Week 3 victory and outscored Rice 24-7 on Saturday night. Not sure they want to lean into that trend in Pullman, however. (Last week: 3)

4. Colorado State (2-2)

Result: lost at UTSA 59-45

Next up: vs. Oregon State (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: A tough assignment in San Antonio was made substantially more difficult without injured quarterback Hauss Hejny (hamstring). But his backup, K’saan Farrar, who followed Jim Mora Jr. from UConn, was more than adequate. The problem, for the second consecutive week, was CSU’s defense. (Last week: 5)

5. Texas State (2-2)

Result: beat Incarnate Word 63-10

Next up: at San Diego State (7:30 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: Had the Bobcats prevented a game-winning touchdown run with 14 seconds remaining by UTSA a few weeks ago, their resume would look markedly different. As we have said many times, the entire feel of a 12-game season typically turns on three or four plays. (Last week: 6)

6. San Diego State (1-3)

Result: lost at Toledo 41-16

Next up: vs. Texas State (7:30 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: The lengthy list of woe in San Diego starts with the absence of defensive coordinator Rob Aurich, who’s now with Nebraska, and the poor quarterback play. Replacing elite coordinators is a tough deal, especially at the Group of Six level. But it was easy to see the quarterback issues coming after Jayden Denegal’s wobbly play last season. (Last week: 4)

7. Washington St. (1-3)

Result: lost to Arizona 34-24

Next up: vs. Fresno State (6:30 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: Because the Cougars have yet to face a Group of Six opponent, it’s difficult to know where they stand relative to the rest of the conference. (Other than Duquesne, their schedule has been arduous). This week offers needed perspective. Our hunch: The product revealed Saturday night will be substandard. (Last week: 7)

8. Utah State (1-3)

Result: beat Troy 21-10

Next up: at Boise State (4:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: There are winnable games remaining for the Aggies. But Boise State is not one of them, even if the Broncos are in letdown mode after their big victory at Western Michigan. (Last week: 8)

Washington State.title: Cougars Fall to Arizona 34-24 in Competitive Matchup
5 lingering thoughts from Cougars' weekend loss to Arizona | WSU Rewind
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Not 10 seconds had passed after Kirby Moore sat down at the podium, ready to discuss his Washington State team’s 34-24 loss to Arizona on Saturday evening, when he summed things up pretty succinctly.

“This should hurt,” Moore said.

That it did for the Cougars, who took an early two-score lead only for it to evaporate in the second half, when the Wildcats outpaced the hosts to the tune of 20-7. Quarterback Caden Pinnick played an OK game, but he also lost two more turnovers, giving him five on the season. And if it weren’t for an Arizona defender falling down in the fourth quarter, WSU would have netted just one offensive touchdown, which came on its opening series.

Here are five thoughts on this WSU loss, which dropped the group to 1-3 to open Moore’s debut season.

1. DE Linus Zunk turns in sharp game

It had been a quiet two games for Vanderbilt transfer Linus Zunk, one half of the pass rush duo that figured to take WSU’s defense from staunch to scary. After turning in four pressures in the season-opening Apple Cup, Zunk went on to have a muted impact in the Cougars’ next three games, posting zero pressures against Kansas State and two against FCS Duquesne.

That changed on Saturday, when Zunk registered his first sack in a WSU uniform, finishing with two pressures total, according to Pro Football Focus. That may sound like a relatively unremarkable day, but think back to WSU safety Jackquintin Bal’s pick-six in the first quarter. Part of the reason Arizona QB Noah Fifita threw such an errant pass, it seemed, was because Zunk produced enough penetration to get a hand in Fifita’s face at the last second.

For the season, Zunk now has eight QB pressures, tied with his pass-rushing partner, Matyus McLain, for the team lead. Zunk has also earned a PFF defensive grade of 70.5, which ranks second among all Cougars playing meaningful snap counts. That’s just about what WSU was looking for from Zunk when coaches recruited him out of the transfer portal.

2. WSU must improve end-of-half operations

For the second straight week, WSU coaches bungled an end-of-half opportunity, missing out on a chance to score a touchdown before halftime. In Saturday’s game, a bevy of things went the Cougars’ way: A late-hit penalty on Arizona, then a pass-interference penalty on Arizona and, three plays later, another 15-yard penalty against the Wildcats. Also sandwiched in there, Pinnick got away with a bad decision to loft the ball downfield – more on that later – because an Arizona defender bobbled an easy interception on his way out of bounds.

That set WSU up with this dream scenario: first-and-10 from the Arizona 12, the game clock at 1:18, which is tons of time. But after running their first play, a QB keeper for Pinnick, they let the clock run down, all the way from 1:15 to 33 seconds, before calling a timeout.

The reasoning remains unclear. The Cougars could have done all kinds of things with that time: run another play, called a quick timeout, you name it. Instead, they cost themselves 40 seconds doing nothing. They paid for it. One play later, Pinnick was sacked, and then on a screen play on third-and-12, Pinnick’s pass was wide of receiver Tank Hawkins Jr., forcing him to retreat and take a loss.

WSU did get points out of that drive, a field goal from struggling kicker Jack Stevens, but the Cougars certainly left something to be desired. To their credit, they did make an effort to move the ball down the field in this 2-minute situation, which they didn’t attempt last week against one of the FCS ranks’ worst defenses.

But considering the array of plays that went WSU’s way in this situation, it stands to reason the Cougars could have gotten a lot more out of that spot.

3. Cougars must clean up their special teams unit as a whole

In this game, Stevens will get dinged for a missed field goal, his fifth in four games. He has been far from perfect, but this one wasn’t his fault. On the play, offensive lineman Jaylin Caldwell failed to really block anyone, letting Arizona defender Tre Smith come through mostly unblocked and get a hand on the ball, knocking it away.

That sowed another seed of doubt in this WSU special teams unit, even with Stevens back improving, which seems to be the case after he nailed a 33-yard field goal later in the game.

In the third quarter, after another forgettable series on offense, WSU punted it back to Arizona. Wildcat receiver Caleb Smith fielded it at his own 30, darted around defenders and scampered upfield, all the way to the Cougars 31, where he was dragged down. It was a 39-yard return, setting up the Wildcats deep in Cougar territory.

It’s not the first time that’s happened to WSU’s punt coverage team. In a road game against Kansas State earlier this month, the Cougars gave up a 62-yard return, which the purple Wildcats turned into a touchdown two plays later. WSU special teams coordinator Derek Sage, who also coaches receivers, hasn’t been able to get much consistency out of that group early in the season.

The only bright spot on WSU’s special teams group has been punter Max Dean, who battled migraines in Saturday’s game to record five punts for 200 total yards, an average of 40 yards. He’s now averaging 45.2 yards per punt, which ranks No. 14 in the country.

4. Pinnick played a solid short game, but he’s shown weaknesses trying to extend plays

In Saturday’s game, Pinnick was at his best completing passes of short-to-intermediate length, tracking with patterns that have surfaced so far this fall. On passes between zero and 9 yards, Pinnick completed 18 of 21 throws, which is an elite percentage of 85%. Credit WSU coaches for putting him in those situations to make his best throws.

But Pinnick now has five turnovers, and many have come when he’s tried to extend plays and do more. Early against Arizona, Pinnick scrambled out of the pocket and flung a pass downfield, where it was easily intercepted by a Wildcat defender. He might not have seen the double coverage in the sun.

Then, in the third quarter, he was facing heavy pressure when he tried to get the ball out. He tried to do so too late, and he lost the ball as he was throwing it, resulting in another turnover for WSU, which has committed seven total this fall. Toss in another iffy decision from Pinnick, on that near-interception in the second frame, and it could have grown to eight.

“We’re all in this together,” Moore said. “So it starts with me, obviously the offensive staff. Just having that dialogue with him, whether it’s in practice on the headset, reminders, making sure he knows exactly the stipulations, or even there on the third down. We ran the quarterback, he slides. That’s an unfortunate one. It’s a QB designed run, and so we got to make sure he’s on the same page with that.”

5. WSU must get more from its running backs

Here are the numbers from Cougar running backs against FBS competition: 50 carries for 169 yards, which comes out to 3.38 yards per carry. Tailbacks Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi were seen as a formidable trio headed into this season, but with the exception of a brilliant day against FCS Duquesne last weekend, they haven’t generated the production to match.

Things figure to get a little easier for WSU next week, when Fresno State comes to town, kicking off Pac-12 play. Those are the games in which we can begin to judge this WSU team in earnest. But against FBS teams, the Cougars’ ground game hasn’t been compelling just yet.

Washington State.title: After loss to Arizona, WSU's offense shows more life, but Cougars must make better decisions | Analysis
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – The beginning of this Washington State season, the gauntlet the Cougars would see to open the Kirby Moore era, was always going to be difficult to parse. They faced three Power 4 teams in their first four games. Two were on the road. One came on a short week.

The Cougars were expected to come away from that stretch with one win and three losses. Thanks to a 34-24 setback to Arizona here on Saturday evening, WSU has fulfilled that much, which is not an indictment on these Cougars. But it does bring up the question that may define the rest of this season.

How many of the problems WSU’s offense is facing are a product of the stiff competition, and how many are the product of self-inflicted wounds that the Cougars would commit against the Pac-12 foes coming up?

We won’t know that much until conference play arrives when WSU hosts Fresno State next weekend, but the early returns on the Cougars’ offense are far from encouraging. Think about this stat, which is now official after Saturday’s game: In three games against FBS competition, WSU has produced three offensive touchdowns and committed six turnovers. The Cougars have lost seven total.

Moore’s team was expected to lose the games it has. It’s the way the Cougs’ offense is costing the team, though, that raises cause for concern.

“We gotta make sure we have a plan that everyone’s on the same page,” Moore said, “going from the half to the third quarter, especially in a tight game like that where our defense is battling, and we gotta find more ways to create explosive plays. We had them in the first quarter, in the first half, and had opportunities there to score even more. And then in the second half, we didn’t. So we gotta look at the film and see where we went wrong.”

In this one, WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick completed 24 of 41 passes for 241 yards, one touchdown and one interception, which came in the first quarter. If an Arizona defender hadn’t bobbled the ball later in the first half, Pinnick would have thrown two. Those were two costly decisions. Consider the other turnover Pinnick lost, a fumble that happened because he tried to throw the ball while being dragged down, and you start to see some of the poor decision-making that has led to Pinnick’s total turnover number this fall: four.

The reason that trend looms large for WSU: Pinnick is committing turnovers because of listless decisions, not because Power 4 athletes are making spectacular plays. Remember his interception last week against FCS Duquesne, when he threw into what became triple coverage downfield? Those are the kinds of poor decisions that have created such a gaping hole in the Cougars’ offense.

It would be one thing if Pinnick was playing a solid brand of football and a freak Power 4 defender, the kind that Arizona and Kansas State can afford, used his strength to jar the ball loose. That would be forgivable. But that’s not what’s happening. It may be Pinnick’s first season of FBS ball, but he has been too slow to differentiate a good decision from a bad one, especially when he’s looking to stretch the field vertically.

That raises a fair question: How can WSU coaches help Pinnick avoid those kinds of turnovers? How can they help Pinnick make better decisions, like in the third quarter, when he slid and gave himself up one yard short of a first down?

“We’re all in this together,” Moore said. “So it starts with me, obviously the offensive staff. Just having that dialogue with him, whether it’s in practice on the headset, reminders, making sure he knows exactly the stipulations, or even there on the third down. We ran the quarterback, he slides. That’s an unfortunate one. It’s a QB-designed run, and so we got to make sure he’s on the same page with that.”

The other problem the Cougars are facing is consistency. Their first drive in Saturday’s game, an 11-play, 71-yard scoring series, was nearly flawless. It ended when Pinnick took a QB keeper 11 yards into the end zone, following a string of perfect blocks, capping a perfect series. If that’s the way the Cougs were going to play in this one, well, the Wildcats should have been on their heels.

But WSU’s offense hardly looked the same after that. In the third quarter, the Cougs put up these numbers: 3 points, 149 total yards, 44 rushing yards, two three-and-outs, four punts and three sacks taken, giving Pinnick 10 sacks taken on the season. That opened the door for Arizona to turn a three-point deficit into a four-point lead, adding two more scoring drives in the fourth frame.

The Cougs can rebound from this. They showed what their offense can look like on that first series, and by showing an increased willingness to take shorter throws, Pinnick looks more than capable of making adjustments. But the biggest one he’ll have to make to avoid meeting the same fate against Pac-12 teams is more about trimming things out of his game.

He’ll have to make better decisions, better calls on when to try to stretch the ball down the field and when to be OK with checking it down. Fresno State’s defense figures to give him more opportunities to show that kind of acumen. But it’s on Pinnick, Moore and offensive coordinator Matt Miller to put themselves in a position where those changes don’t become just possible, they become probable.

“Give Arizona credit; they have a unique scheme,” Moore said. “So there was different variations of zone, whether it was inside, outside. Obviously, the quarterback pin-pull there we scored on in the first quarter. So there were some ID things there. Give them a ton of credit with how fast and hard those guys played. But we gotta have an answer as well with protecting the quarterback and having some more opportunities in the pass game.”

Washington State.title: Long stretch of offensive malaise dooms Washington State in loss to Arizona | Instant reactions
Washington State.summary:
It was a dream start for Washington State against its old Pac-12 foes from Arizona. The Cougars built a two-touchdown lead in the first quarter after a stellar opening possession and a pick-six.

But the Wildcats rallied, and WSU began to lose steam in the second half. Arizona contained the Cougs’ offense, and too much was asked of the WSU defense, which eventually faded. The Wildcats scored on their final four drives to close out a 34-24 win over WSU on Saturday at Gesa Field in Pullman.

A long time between TDs

WSU’s first drive of the game was inspiring. It surely had fans wondering if the Cougars had found the recipe for offensive success after the unit struggled in its first two games against FBS opponents.

The Cougs coasted downfield with precision, scoring on quarterback Caden Pinnick’s 11-yard keeper to cap a 10-play, 71-yard drive. The passing game was fluid, with quick throws to the sideline most effective. The tempo game was working.

But the Cougs couldn’t maintain that level of flow offensively. Not by a long shot. The Cougars’ first five drives of the second half resulted in 22 net yards on 20 plays. WSU punted four times and Pinnick lost a fumble on a sack during that stretch. That allowed Arizona to gradually build its lead.

WSU’s offense didn’t score another touchdown until a prayer was answered midway through the fourth quarter – a 46-yard touchdown pass on a fourth-and-10 to Branden Ganashamoorthy, which cut the Arizona lead to 31-24 and gave WSU life after it appeared the game was out of reach.

Before WSU’s last two possessions, the team had barely surpassed 200 total yards.

The Cougs’ ground game was largely ineffective (3.1 yards per carry on 30 attempts). Arizona’s blitzing became more impactful as the game wore on, and Pinnick seemed like he was constantly under pressure. Does that explain the Cougs’ offensive fall-off after the first series? Whatever the case, WSU showed that it can have a capable offense. It just needs to find a way to sustain it for more than one drive.

Credit to the defense

Star Arizona quarterback Noah Fifita was gifted short fields on the Wildcats’ first two possessions of the second half – lousy punt return coverage by WSU set up Arizona at the WSU 33, then Pinnick lost a fumble at his own 32.

The Wildcats didn’t score on either drive. WSU’s defense stuffed two runs and came up with an open-field tackle to force a three-and-out on the first one, and Arizona missed a 42-yard field goal. The Cougars showed more impressive open-field tackling on the next Arizona series, and a low kick on a 43-yard field goal try was blocked by WSU’s Damarjhe Lewis.

The Cougs’ defense accounted for seven of WSU’s 17 first-half points – Jackquintin Bal made a heady interception and returned it for a touchdown – and the unit kept the game in reach as WSU’s offense continued to stall.

Finally, as the fourth quarter approached, WSU’s defense couldn’t hold any longer. The group had just been on the field too much and was clearly getting tired.

Fifita, as a fifth-year player should do, started to find the cracks, and Arizona scored 20 points over its final four possessions – though it should be noted that the Cougar defense came up with a big stand on Arizona’s final drive, stuffing three consecutive runs to force a 51-yard field goal attempt. But the kick sailed through, dashing WSU’s hopes of tying the game on its final drive.

Some positives for WSU’s defense: It held Arizona to less than 3 yards per carry through three quarters before the Wildcats amassed 93 yards on the ground in the fourth; Fifita, one of the nation’s top passers, was thrown off his game on six of Arizona’s 12 possessions and completed a season-low 61% of his passes, and the Cougs’ pass rush got home for three sacks.

Otherwise, just a few too many explosive plays allowed. Fifita and receiver Tre Spivey, who had a career day in the first half alone with 125 yards and two TDs, connected for four passing plays of 18 or more yards before halftime. When WSU’s defense adjusted and covered Spivey up, Fifita found Caleb Smith on back-to-back deep balls of 41 and 38 yards. There were some clear miscommunications in the secondary for WSU.

More of these games, please

It’s uncertain whether WSU, now effectively relegated to the Group of Six, can bring more former Pac-12 rivals to Pullman for nonconference games in future seasons. But if at all possible, the Cougars should make it happen.

These games feel important, giving the Cougars a chance to show that they’re still more than capable of competing with Big 12/Pac-12 legacy programs like Arizona.

For the most part, it was an entertaining and well-matched game, and evoked some feeling of “Pac-12 After Dark” nostalgia, though it – thankfully – didn’t kick off at 8 p.m.

Certainly, the WSU/Arizona matchup was one of the three most highly anticipated games on the Cougs’ schedule, alongside the Apple Cup and the Oct. 24 home game against Boise State.

Washington State.title: Arizona quarterback Noah Fifita shows command, closes out game | Difference makers
Washington State.summary:
Arizona QB Noah Fifita

The Wildcats’ veteran quarterback overcame a slow start, guiding back-to-back touchdown drives to erase a 14-point deficit in the first half. Fifita unlocked the Arizona offense again after an uneven start to the third quarter, connecting with Caleb Smith on a 41-yard deep ball, then hit Smith on the next play for a 38-yard TD. Early in the fourth quarter, Fifita fired a pinpoint over-the-shoulder pass to Isaiah Mizell for an 11-yard TD. The fifth-year Wildcat QB showed poise and command in the later stages, leading four consecutive scoring drives to close the game. He finished 22 of 36 for 297 yards and four TDs, improving to 2-0 in Pullman. Fifita’s first win as a starting QB came in 2023 at WSU.

WSU S Jackquintin Bal

The junior Arizona native produced the top highlight for a Cougars defense that showed cracks but also made a number of stops against Arizona’s explosive offense. Late in the first quarter, Fifita tried to fit an intermediate throw into a tight window, and Bal read the play perfectly. He darted forward to gain positioning and cut off the pass for an interception, then raced untouched 25 yards for a pick-six, putting WSU ahead 14-0. In the fourth quarter, Bal nearly had another takeaway, getting his hands on a lofted ball to the Cougs’ end zone for a PBU. Bal, an Arizona State transfer, led the team with a career-high nine tackles (six solo), making a handful of difficult, open-field stops.

Washington State.title: Washington State lets lead slip away against Arizona | Recap and highlights
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN — Linebacker Keith Brown lowered his head and raised his fist, another third-down stop firmly in his Washington State team’s grasp. It was getting late in Saturday night’s affair, a legacy Pac-12 matchup between WSU and Arizona at Gesa Field, and the Cougars had just forced their guests into a short field goal. Music blared. Fans bellowed.

Could the Cougs’ offense, now down seven points, take advantage?

WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick and his unit certainly made things interesting, scoring on a long touchdown midway through the fourth quarter, but it wasn’t enough for the Cougars to avoid a 34-24 loss to the Wildcats, who iced this win with a long field goal with about two minutes to play.

All things considered, it was the best effort of the season for WSU, which concludes nonconference play with the 1-3 record it was expected to, but Arizona won the second half, 20-7. Pinnick completed 24 of 41 passes for 241 yards, one touchdown and one interception for WSU, which scored twice outside of its opening series, a field goal from kicker Jack Stevens and a touchdown pass from Pinnick to receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, who took advantage of an Arizona defender who had fallen down.

Pinnick also lost a fumble, giving him five turnovers in his first four games at WSU. The Cougars have now lost seven total turnovers this fall, a key reason behind many of the struggles of offensive coordinator Matt Miller’s unit.

The Cougars, who managed 154 total yards in the second half, still had a chance in the fourth quarter. At one point, Arizona scored on three straight drives to take a 31-17 advantage, seemingly putting the game away. But about halfway through the frame, Pinnick dropped back and spotted Ganashamoorthy, who sprung open thanks to a stumble from his defender. The Cougs drew within seven with seven minutes to play.

But with a chance to get a stop and give their offense the ball back, the Cougars’ defense couldn’t push the Wildcats out of field goal range for kicker Michael Salgado-Medina, who nailed one from 51 yards. That gave Arizona the final margin with a shade under two minutes to play.

All told, the Cougars were undone by their offense’s inability to adjust to the Wildcats’ pass rush. For the game, Pinnick took three sacks, giving him 10 on the season. WSU also managed just 94 rushing yards, and if you pare that down to production from running backs, the number drops to 59. In the end, the Cougars ran out of answers on that side of the ball.

WSU looked sharp to open the game, capping a flawless opening drive with an 11-yard touchdown rush from Pinnick, who looked to be in control of his offense. Then moments later, transfer safety Jackquintin Ball jumped in front of a pass from Arizona QB Noah Fifita and returned it 25 yards for a touchdown, giving his team a 14-0 lead in the opening minutes of the game. Gesa Field roared its approval.

From there, though, WSU couldn’t generate the same level of production. Fifita — who completed 22 of 36 passes for 297 yards, four touchdowns and the one interception — easily led the Wildcats to back-to-back touchdown drives to tie the game back up at 14-14. His favorite target was receiver Tre Spivey, who hauled in both of those scoring passes en route to a big night: Seven catches for 129 yards and the two scores.

It was a forgettable night for the Cougars’ secondary, which was gashed for seven passes of 15-plus yards, including a 44-yard completion and a 41-yarder. WSU safety Jaylen Thomas has blossomed into one of his group’s best players, but chalk this one up as a learning moment for the redshirt sophomore.

In this one, WSU kicker Jack Stevens made his first field goal since the Sept. 6 Apple Cup, cashing in from 33 yards. But thanks to shoddy blocking on his first attempt, he missed one earlier, making him 2-for-7 on the year.

WSU returns to action next Saturday for the beginning of Pac-12 play, hosting Fresno State. It’ll be the teams’ first meeting in Pullman since 1994.

Pinnick totaled 51 passing yards on the Cougars’ opening drive.

Halftime

The Wildcats rallied to tie the game due in large part to the performance of Tre Spivey. The Arizona wide receiver has 125 yards and two touchdowns so far.

Pregame

Washington State will engage in some nostalgia this weekend, hosting fellow Pac-12 legacy program Arizona.

Senior quarterback Noah Fifita and the Wildcats are 2-1 this season. Arizona has comfortable wins against Northern Arizona (35-7) and Northern Illinois (42-17), but lost an early-season test against ninth-ranked BYU (28-17).

The Cougars (1-2) are fresh off their first win of the season, a second-half domination of Duquesne 48-7. They will try to carry that momentum into a primetime game against Arizona, the Cougars’ final tuneup before Pac-12 Conference play starts on Oct. 3.

For Washington State to find success, quarterback Caden Pinnick will have to execute against Arizona, especially from play-action. Paul Hutson and the rest of Washington State’s defense will try to slow down Fifita and the rest of Arizona’s offense.

The game is scheduled to kick off at 4:30 p.m. on CBS.

Series history

Washington State is 19-28 all-time against Arizona. The Wildcats won the last matchup 44-6 in Pullman on Oct. 14, 2023.

Notable stat

Arizona quarterback Noah Fifita has faced pressure in the pocket on 23% of plays. Fifita has completed 7 of 12 passes for 67 yards and one interception in pressure situations so far this season.

Washington State.title: WSU punter Max Dean gametime decision against Arizona
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN — Washington State’s special teams unit may not be at full strength for Saturday’s game against Arizona.

Cougar punter Max Dean is dealing with migraines and will be a gametime decision, a source told The Spokesman-Review, which would be a costly development for WSU. Dean is averaging 45 yards per punt, which ranks No. 18 nationally.

At around 3:15 p.m. Saturday, Dean emerged from the locker room for warmups, signaling he may be able to play. If not, look for kicker Jack Stevens to take over punting duties. Dean also holds kicks, but it’s unclear who would take over that job.

Kickoff is set for 4:30 p.m. on CBS.

A transfer from New Mexico, Dean has punted 14 times for 627 yards in three games this season, which translates to 44.8 yards per punt. His longest punt covered 52 yards, and he’s landed five inside the 20-yard line, including both of his punts last weekend against FCS Duquesne. 

“One thing I think is getting overshadowed is just how well Max Dean is doing in the punt game,” WSU coach Kirby Moore said on Monday. “I know he had two there inside the 10, so really good job by him being consistent so far this season.”

WSU is also looking to get more out of Stevens, who has opened the season 1-for-5 on field goals, including missing the first extra point of his career last weekend. In his college career, which he started at South Dakota State in 2024, he has never punted. The last time he did was in high school.

Washington State.title: WSU fought until the bell but couldn't find knockout punch against Arizona | Jacob Thorpe
Washington State.summary:
The problem with boxing’s rope-a-dope technique, made famous by Muhammad Ali and perfected by Homer Simpson, is at some point you have to punch back.

Washington State welcomed a former Pac-10/12 rival, now with the Big 12, back to Pullman, for a messy, physical grudge match. Before the game CBS sports relished in rehashing the history of Arizona’s star quarterback, Noah Fifita, whose starting debut was a 44-6 route in Pullman over the 19th-ranked Cougars in 2023.

But the final trip to Pullman wouldn’t be so pretty. The Cougars did what they needed to give themselves a chance with an offense that is still finding its way. The game was a sloppy slugfest, one that featured blocked kicks and straight misses by both teams.

WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick was many miles from good, but he bounced back well from mistakes, at first. If one squinted in the first half, one could see the capability he must have exhibited when winning Big Sky Freshman of the Year honors at UC Davis last year.

The defense began the game by forcing a three-and-out, and almost had a second following the offense’s ensuring touchdown drive. They gave that up on third-and-nine, but held firm and got the ball back, eventually.

The benefit of a low-scoring, high-friction game for an underdog, which WSU was on Saturday, is that one key play or mistake can make the difference. That could have come courtesy of safety Jackquintin Bal, an Arizona native whose exceptional break on a Fifita pass put him in position to intercept the pass, put the intended receiver on his behind, and dance into the end zone to give the home team a 14-0 lead.

With the way the defense was suffocating Arizona at that point, one might think they could pull this off. Absorb the Wildcats’ best shots, do that rope-a-dope, hold them down long enough and walk out with a gritty, low-scoring win.

Arizona scored 31 of the next 34 points.

A problem that is turning into a pattern for the Cougars is stellar defensive play that wears down over the course of the game. In addition to the first quarter interception, the Cougars sacked Fifita on each of Arizona’s first two drives. The defensive linemen’s long arms were up and active in passing lanes and creating chaos for the diminutive Arizona quarterback.

WSU got one more shot when an ill-advised Arizona blitz led to a wide-open Branden Ganashamoorthy, whose 46-yard touchdown reception brought WSU within seven of the Wildcats.

The Cougars have some great defensive players, but it does not appear to have enough depth to sustain that level of play all game. Particularly when the offense is not giving them much time to rest in between drives.

The solace for WSU is that things are, probably, about to get a mite easier. The Cougars have only lost to Power Four teams at this point, and there aren’t any left on the schedule. The Cougars should have one of the better defenses in the Pac-12.

But as we’ve already seen, no matter how good the defense is, WSU won’t win many games if the offense can’t manage a punch.
