Washington State.title: Why Arizona will beat Washington State | The pick
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – For a moment, let’s be frank about Washington State’s most recent game, a home blowout win over Duquesne.

The Cougars beat a bad FCS team, which entered allowing some of the most yards in the country. WSU coach Kirby Moore did well to make key adjustments, especially those on offense, which should encourage scores of fans. Quarterback Caden Pinnick looked excellent in the second half, and thanks to running backs Maxwell Woods and Kirby Vorhees, the hosts looked like a juggernaut in the second half.

But as WSU prepares to host Arizona in primetime on Saturday, we must keep this in mind: In two games against FBS competition, the Cougars have managed one touchdown and four turnovers. Their offense has looked meager at best.

That’s no way to topple Arizona as a 10½-point underdog, which is a key reason why we’re picking the Wildcats to beat the Cougars.

Look for Arizona to win a close game at Gesa Field.

But here’s what’s important: This isn’t to say the Cougars have no chance. In fact, far from it. Thanks to a few shrewd adjustments, their offense looks far different than it did even a few weeks ago. Moore has shared some input in the playcalling department, WSU has shuffled its offensive line and Woods has gotten more opportunities to attack on the ground.

The Cougs should feel encouraged by those changes, which should help them win several Pac-12 games this season. But here’s predicting it won’t be enough to win a game against a Big 12 foe, especially with speedy wide receiver Tony Freeman out for the season with an injury.

Final score: Arizona 23, WSU 16

Washington State.title: WSU's keys to victory against Arizona | Two-minute drill
Washington State.summary:
Washington State vs. Arizona

Saturday, 4:30 p.m.

Line: Arizona favored by 10½

TV: CBS Radio: 920-AM

Key matchup

WSU offense against Arizona defense: Even after a convincing win over FCS Duquesne last weekend, the Cougars’ offense still has something to prove against FBS competition. In their two games against defenses in that category, WSU has scored one offensive touchdown against four turnovers. The Cougs made some nice adjustments to earn their first win of the season, but whether they can keep those up against the Wildcats’ defense will play an outsize role in the outcome of Saturday’s game.

The Cougars will need to play clean football against the Wildcats’ defense, which has forced just one turnover in three games this season. WSU will likely roll out the same offensive line as last week – left tackle Ashton Tripp, left guard Jonny Lester, center Noah Dunham, right guard Nick Bakken and right tackle Jaylin Caldwell – which helped the Cougars rack up more than 300 rushing yards against Duquesne. They won’t need to match that total on Saturday, but they’ll need to present a credible rushing game to keep the Wildcats’ defense honest.

How the Cougs win …

To limit Arizona’s high-powered offense, WSU could use a turnover or two, which safety Jaylen Thomas has shown he’s capable of doing. He picked off two passes against Kansas State, including a pick-six right before halftime, and he can do something similar against Arizona QB Noah Fifita, the hosts will have a much better chance at springing the upset.

The Cougars will also need to get pressure on Fifita, who has already taken eight sacks in three games. WSU pass rushers Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk are still looking for their first sacks of the season, and with backups Mike Hughes and Malachi Wrice out, they’ll bear most of the responsibility on that front.

Only one problem for WSU: Arizona ranks No. 18 nationally in Pro Football Focus’ pass-blocking grades. The only sacks the Wildcats’ offensive line have given up are three from left guard Rhino Tapa’atoutai, which could give WSU defensive linemen Paul Hutson III and Kaden Beatty some opportunities.

How the Wildcats win …

Arizona has lots of paths to a win, but the most probable involves the way it has won two games this fall: by dominating on offense. Fifita has become one of the nation’s most prolific passers, completing better than 80% of his throws for eight touchdowns, and he is looking more and more comfortable on the ground . He’s broken off a 30-yard rush, which is the longest of his career.

But Fifita and the Wildcats may not have their full complement of playmakers in Saturday’s game. Receiver Giovanni Richardson, who leads the team in receiving despite missing last weekend’s game with an injury, is questionable to play against WSU. The Wildcats also produced just 84 rushing yards against Northern Illinois, which prompted coach Brent Brennan to address that earlier this week.

“We’re aggressively attacking that,” Brennan said, “because it’s unacceptable where it’s at right now.”

Key stat: 23%

Fifita has faced pressure in the pocket on 23% of passing plays this season, according to Pro Football Focus. In those situations, Fifita has completed 7 of 12 passes for 67 yards and one interception, the only pick he’s thrown. If Fifita has shown any vulnerability this season, it’s been when he’s under duress, which makes it even more important that McLain and Zunk create havoc in the backfield.

Quotable

“I feel like attention to detail,” WSU linebacker DJ Warner said about the biggest differences between his team’s difference from Week 1 to Week 4. “I feel like as far as the defense and the whole team in general, I feel like now we’re way more detail-oriented than we were in Week 1, and I feel like that’s gonna be the thing that really helps us take it to the next level.”

Washington State.title: How WSU can pull an upset on visiting Arizona in a primetime matchup
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – When DJ Warner was growing up in the Phoenix area, in between the dry heat and the desert views he got to know Arizona’s football program .

The Wildcats are based about two hours away from Warner’s hometown of Glendale, but thanks to the relatively close distance he formed something of a relationship with their coaches during the first stages of his recruitment.

Warner is now at his third stop of his college football journey – starting at linebacker for Washington State – but he still remembers some of the friendships he formed in those days. Many stayed in the area. Some even landed at Arizona.

“It’s gonna be great to see them after the game,” Warner said.

Warner will hope that when he sees his old buddies after WSU’s home showdown with Arizona, set for 4:30 p.m. Saturday on CBS, he won’t just be smiling because he’s happy to see them. He’ll hope he’s happy because his Cougars pulled an upset in primetime.

There’s a lot on the line this weekend for WSU, which is aiming for its second straight win following a home blowout over Duquesne last week. For Kirby Moore to avoid a 1-3 start in his debut season, which would put his program’s sparkly bowl streak in peril, Moore will have to prepare his team for the scintillating offense the Wildcats have ridden to a 2-1 start to the season.

“I think our guys have done a good job being where their feet are. That’s been the most important thing for us this week,” Moore said, whose team enters as a 10½-point underdog. “Really good meetings, walk-through, practice, control the things you can. It’s gonna be a great challenge on Saturday.”

It’s a legacy Pac-12 tilt for Arizona and WSU, who scheduled this nonconference affair back in January 2025, about a year and a half after the traditional conference collapsed and the Wildcats joined the Big 12. Arizona won the last meeting, a blowout win in Pullman in 2023, but the Cougars have won five of the past seven clashes. If you look past the 2023 game, you would have to flip the calendar back to 2014 to find the last time the Wildcats walked out of Pullman with a win.

Can WSU (1-2) keep that trend up? Here’s the interesting part about one of the keys to the game, which will be whether the Cougs can defang Arizona QB Noah Fifita and his playmakers: WSU defensive coordinator Trent Bray, who will lead the charge on that front, is no stranger to the Wildcats’ staff. Back in 2012-14, when Bray was a linebackers coach and graduate assistant at Oregon State, he got to know Arizona coach Brent Brennan, who was the Beavers’ wide receivers coach at the time.

Brennan, who called Bray “a really good friend of mine,” also had this to say this week about his old buddy at OSU: “He’s Uncle Trent to my kids. We’ve had a lot of fun together. Trent is an outstanding football coach.”

But on Saturday, Bray and the Cougars’ defense will have their hands full with the Wildcats’ offense, which put up 42 points in a lopsided win over Northern Illinois last weekend. The tip of the spear is Fifita, who has completed 81% of his passes for 834 yards, seven touchdowns and just one interception, leading his club to a season-opening win over FCS Northern Arizona before falling in a close loss to top-15 BYU the following weekend.

Fifita, who set a program record for career touchdown passes last Saturday, used that 2023 win over WSU to continue what turned into a breakout year. Three years later, he’s still running the show at Arizona (2-1), whose passing offense has been the strength of the team. The Wildcats’ 306 passing yards per game ranks No. 20 nationwide, including third in the Big 12.

“Very accurate passer, ton of completions, can extend plays. He’s a playmaker,” Moore said of Fifita. “We gotta play team defense. Trust your teammate that he’s doing his job. Sometimes you try and force something or you’re pressing, and he’s able to extend the play and then find guys downfield.”

But there’s more to the story on Arizona’s offense. One of the Wildcats’ top receivers, Giovanni Richardson, is questionable to play on Saturday thanks to a lower-body injury. He missed his group’s last game. Despite that absence, he retains the team’s best receiving numbers, hauling in 14 catches for 161 yards.

If Giovanni can’t go on Saturday, look for receivers Tre Spivey and Isaiah Mizell to get more reps. Regardless, WSU may not be at full strength at cornerback, where starter Jalil Tucker will be a game-time decision due to injury. Tucker has missed the last two games, and if that becomes three, the Cougars may be forced to move nickelback Jamarey Smith to cornerback, which is the approach they took last weekend against Duquesne.

WSU also has something to prove on offense. After their first two outings, road losses to Washington and Kansas State, the Cougars ranked last nationally in total offense and points per game. Quarterback Caden Pinnick and the Cougars’ offense rebounded nicely in a blowout win over winless FCS club Duquesne, but the Wildcats’ will bear many more similarities to the kinds of defenses WSU will face when Pac-12 play begins the following week.

Here’s another key to Saturday’s game: How does kicker Jack Stevens fare? After opening the season 1-for-5 on field goals, including a missed extra point last weekend, Stevens is off to a rocky start. Moore has expressed confidence in his kicker, but if the Cougars face a fourth-and-manageable on the Wildcats’ side of the field, what will they do? Keep a close eye on that pattern.

Either way, WSU has lots to play for in Saturday’s game, even outside of looking good in a primetime slot on national TV. To earn bowl eligibility, which they’ve secured in 10 of the last 11 full seasons, the Cougars could really use this win over the Wildcats. Otherwise, they’ll be looking at the program’s first 1-3 start in five years.

To avoid that fate, they could get a little boost from Warner and Bray, two of the men who are more familiar with this matchup than others in their program.

“It’s big for me,” Warner said of Bray’s help on the sideline during games. “I’m someone who wants instant feedback. I’m able to go through a play and then instantly look at him to see his reaction, kinda see if I did something right or did something wrong, and then if I did something wrong, I’m able to go to the sideline and instantly correct it. So it’s been big. It’s been very helpful to have somebody who knows the game as much as him in my corner.”

Washington State.title: Yes, blowouts have increased (we have the data), plus CFP expansion, Pac-12 strategy, TV ratings and more | Mailbag
Washington State.summary:
The Hotline mailbag publishes weekly. Please send questions to wilnerhotline@bayareanewsgroup.com and include “mailbag” in the subject line. Or hit me on the social media platform X: @WilnerHotline. Some questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.

It feels like the early season mismatches in college football are becoming even more lopsided. Are they? Is NIL widening the gap between each level of play? — @mattkreuter

Yes, they are. The barrage of blowouts witnessed in Week 1 has continued through the month, and we have the data to prove it.

But let’s first set the stage for this important, unfortunate and somewhat layered development.

The structural changes to the talent acquisition process (e.g., the transfer portal, revenue sharing and NIL) have played a role in the expanding competitive gap, but there is another factor: Fear. Or laziness. Or whatever you call the motivation for schools from the power conferences, especially the Big Ten, to schedule fewer and fewer games against their peers in other power conferences.

The Hotline has drilled into this topic previously, but it’s worth repeating: 28 percent of the Big Ten does not face an opponent from the ACC, Big 12 and SEC this season.

And yes, we are happy to name names: Nebraska, Indiana, USC, Washington and Penn State all took the easy way out.

Between the five schools, there were 15 non-conference slots. All 15 were filled by opponents from the Group of Six or FCS.

It’s embarrassing, frankly.

The Big Ten office isn’t happy — don’t forget: the campuses control their non-conference schedules — and the Big Ten’s media partners (Fox, NBC and CBS) certainly aren’t happy.

The weak sauce is responsible for Fox airing Ohio State-Kent State in its No. 1 broadcast window (Big Noon) last weekend.

The dearth of Power Four vs. Power Four games isn’t limited to the Big Ten, but it’s the primary villain.

Another component to consider when assessing the competitive landscape across the FBS: There are more teams (138) than there were a decade ago. More teams in the pool combined with fewer marquee matchups contributes to the increase in the frequency of blowouts.

And that increase is substantial.

Before we dive in, please note the following data was provided to the Hotline from Sportradar via the Associated Press.

Okay, let’s start broadly:

• Through Week 3, the average point differential in non-conference games involving the ACC, Big 12, Big Ten and SEC teams (plus Notre Dame) was 27.8 points. That’s the largest differential since at least 2000.

And in 2001, the margin was 13.2 points through three weeks, so it has more than doubled.

But if we filter, the trend becomes more pronounced:

• The differential cited above (27.8 points) includes Power Four vs. Power Four games. When you remove those matchups and focus solely on instances of Power Four teams facing Group of Six/FCS opponents, the average margin jumps to 34.6 points.

Which is the largest since the tracking process began a quarter century ago.

In fact, the average differential in Power Four vs. Group of Six/FCS games has climbed steadily over five years:

2022: 26.7

2023: 26.9

2024: 29.1

2025: 31.1

2026: 34.6

The trend is clear, and so is the math: The five-year increase of 29.6 percent coincides with NIL becoming law of the land in the summer of 2021, plus the start of unlimited, penalty-free transfers in the spring of 2024 and, finally, revenue sharing in the summer of 2025.

Those changes to the economic and roster-construction models reward schools with the deepest pockets and allow the talent to flow up the food chain like never before.

The sport is flattening at the top, with more teams than ever before capable of winning the national championship in a given year.

But it’s also thinning out top to bottom, with expanding gaps between the SEC and Big Ten on the highest tier, the ACC and Big 12 on the middle tier and the Group of Six on the lowest.

In our view, the new landscape is roughly the shape of a mushroom cloud.

A new strength-of-schedule metric for the College Football Playoff selection process was announced Thursday. Hypothetically, who gets in between an 11-2 Boise State or undefeated team from any other Group of Six – @NateJones2009

Those issues might not be as interconnected as it appears.

Yes, the CFP unveiled a new metric Thursday that can best be described as strength-of-conference. It joins strength-of-schedule (self-explanatory) and strength-of-record, which compares how Team X fared against its schedule to how an average Top 25 team would perform against the same schedule, in the selection committee’s toolbox.

Strength-of-conference is not an entirely new datapoint for the committee, but it will lend clarity to a vexing issue: How to differentiate teams within a conference given the unbalanced schedules resulting from differences in opponent rotations.

For instance, in the Big Ten, which has 18 teams but only nine conference games, Penn State does not play Ohio State, Oregon or Indiana. Meanwhile, USC plays all three.

Granted, a contrast of that nature would be reflected in the teams’ strength-of-schedule ratings, but strength-of-conference provides an additional layer to the complications caused by mega-conferences.

It won’t be as useful if the committee is forced to evaluate 11-2 Boise State against, say, 13-0 Tulsa or 13-0 James Madison. In that situation, strength-of-schedule and strength-of-record likely will provide the vital data.

In that scenario, the strength of the undefeated team’s non-conference schedule will receive intense scrutiny. If it’s filled with cupcakes and compares poorly to Boise State’s stout lineup (Oregon, Memphis, South Dakota and Western Michigan), the Broncos could very well have the advantage.

Don’t forget: Every aspect of the selection process is relative.

The committee is evaluating multiple resumes for every spot, and that includes the berth reserved for the top team in the Group of Six.

Did the Pac-12 stay at eight teams (for football) with the intention of possibly adding more legacy Pac-12 schools down the road? I have a hard time seeing Stanford and Cal staying on the East Coast. The ‘Pac-8’ plus Cal-ford is better. – @puffboxdaddy

If you were hoping for a definitive yes or no response, the Hotline is sorry to disappoint. The answer is yes and no.

The Pac-12 halted expansion at eight football-playing members because it could not find a ninth school that both met the competitive and financial thresholds and wanted to join the conference.

UNLV turned down an invitation – not a smart decision, by the way – and so did the American trio of Tulane, Memphis and USF.

Texas State made sense as the eighth football school, but there isn’t an obvious fit available. That is the ‘no’ portion of our response: The conference didn’t stop at eight expressly to leave space for Pac-12 legacy schools.

But the desire to remain lean and mean in case another realignment wave strikes in three or five years was definitely part of the broad strategic calculation.

The conference wants to provide a viable option for Cal or Stanford or any other Pac-12 legacy team – or for the top schools in the American.

There is no way to predict whether realignment will hit in the early 2030s or what form it will take. But the Pac-12 is a more desirable landing spot with eight or nine football schools than it would have with 11 or 12 and a bottom tier that didn’t clear the competitive bar.

More meat, less fat was the right call.

That said, Cal and Stanford assuredly will look elsewhere if the ACC implodes, with the Big Ten as their first choice.

We don’t envision them joining the Pac-12 as the conference is currently constructed. For better or worse, they don’t want to be associated academically with the schools hat are now members.

Do the NIL contracts require players to participate in bowl games, or are they still allowing opt-out provisions? – Michael

This issue is sure to surface when we get to the bowl season and can be revisited in-depth at that point. But a summation now seems beneficial.

No, the NIL deals cannot require bowl participation because – and this is often lost in the public discourse – they are not employment contracts.

In fact, the NIL deals are not between the players and the schools; they are between the players and third-party entities.

Not all contracts are structured in the same fashion, but none of them can prevent players from opting out or void the NIL deals in the event a player decides to skip his bowl game.

Always remember, NIL is not pay-for-play … except that it is.

With the College Football Playoff possibly expanding to 24 teams, why is the SEC so set against it? I would think they would want to have the possibility of fielding more teams. – @BolfMike

SEC coaches are in favor of 24 for that very reason: They want enhanced access because it means job security and performance bonuses and contract extensions. And many SEC athletic directors feel the same way.

The 24-team field has support in the ACC, Big 12 and Big Ten for those very reasons, not because it’s indisputably better for the sport.

But SEC commissioner Greg Sankey has been the lone voice of reason in this process, and he would not have staked out that position without support from his presidents.

Before committing to 24, Sankey wants clarity on the TV revenue component: Will the new inventory (12 games) generate enough cash to offset the elimination of the SEC championship, which generates roughly $100 million and would become obsolete with the expanded CFP.

Also, Sankey wisely wants to understand, to the greatest extent possible, the impact a 24-team playoff would have on the regular season.

After all, the SEC’s media partner, ESPN, reaps enormous benefits from the huge audiences that watch SEC (and other) games every fall.

With a 24-team playoff, marquee matchups like USC-Oregon and LSU-Texas A&M would lose much of their drama.

Our hunch is that enough media money will become available from the new inventory – Fox wants to be involved; CBS and NBC may, as well – that Sankey eventually approves the move to 24.

The deadline to inform ESPN of format changes for the 2027 season is Dec. 1, although that potentially could be extended into January, as it was last year.

How does any player who hasn’t entered the portal timely become eligible to play NCAA sports? What stops any player from getting a temporary restraining order? Why would a conference rule be any stronger than the NCAA rules? – H Hughes

It appears the crux of your question is this: Why would the SEC and Big Ten be better equipped to enforce rules under a self-governing model than the NCAA?

That is a rich topic – and one that foreshadows the post-PCSA world.

The Protect College Sports Act is expected to pass the Senate but faces a steep climb in the House of Representatives.

The Big Ten and SEC have made their feelings clear: If the bill fizzles along the legislative process, Plan B is to break away from the NCAA’s governing umbrella and create their own rules around eligibility, tampering, athlete compensation and other issues.

(To be clear: self-governance does not mean exclusively intra-conference competition.)

But policing your own is a precarious business. The schools are genetically engineered to look for every competitive advantage, even if that means breaking the rules.

Would the SEC punish Texas? Would the Big Ten sanction Ohio State? And would any penalties hold up in court if the offending school sought legal relief?

So far, self-governance is 2-for-2: The Big 12 pushed back in federal court against Texas Tech in the Brendan Sorsby affair; and the SEC pushed back on LSU earlier this month when the Tigers tried to roster former NFL players.

In both cases, the authority of the conference was reinforced.

We suspect the individual leagues would have more success in court – yes, even district courts – than the NCAA because they are not national organizations. No single conference controls the market.

Also, the Big Ten and SEC don’t have the paper trail of hypocrisy, obstinance, loopholes and legal losses that the NCAA carries into each court case like three tons of bricks.

If the PCSA fails, self-governance is likely the next step, and it will be fascinating.

How are TV ratings so far this season? Are they better or worse than previous years? – MrEd315

The sample size in 2026 is far too small for conclusions, but we can offer a morsel of context.

Last year, the first four weeks of the season (including Week 0) generated five games with at least 10 million viewers and 10 games with at least five million viewers, according to data published by sportsmediawatch.com.

This year, the first four weeks have produced two games of 10 million viewers and nine games of five million.

So the heavily-watched categories are essentially the same and the mega-watched categories tilts to last year.

Why the disparity in the mega-watched games? The schedule is an important piece. There were more circle-the-date matchups early last season, especially on the Labor Day weekend.

That doesn’t mean the trend will continue, but it’s certainly worth watching.

College football fans might recall all the attention placed on the soaring ratings in 2025, as compared to the 2024 figures, but that was somewhat misleading.

As the Hotline detailed last winter, Nielsen changed its audience-tracking methodology in a manner that benefitted college football. (Nutshell version: It began including college towns in the tracking.)

The year-over-year figures were bound to soar because more viewers were being captured by Nielsen – but they were not necessarily new viewers.

That same methodology is in place this season, allowing an apples-to-apples comparison between 2025 and 2026. We shall see what the data reveal come January.

Washington State.title: Inside the long journey that led DT Paul Hutson to WSU: 'The younger version of myself would be very proud'
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Paul Hutson III likes to say he does best with visual reminders, with illustrations of the goals he’s trying to reach. It’s the reason his X profile picture is the Bronko Nagurski Trophy – awarded to the nation’s top defensive player. It’s the reason he keeps a photo of the NFL draft stage handy on his phone.

It’s also the reason why, in the Gesa Field locker room after he helped his Washington State defense shut down FCS Duquesne last weekend, he pulled out his phone. He did a Google search for photos of Noah Fifita, Arizona’s quarterback, found one he liked and saved it .

He then made it his lock screen wallpaper, swapping out a photo of Carson Camp, the quarterback that WSU had just taken down.

“It’s just constant visual reminders of things helping me achieve my goals that I set out for myself,” Hutson said.

You see, Hutson has started a tradition for himself this season, his final year of college football. Before the season, he made a list of all the quarterbacks WSU was likely to face this fall: Demond Williams Jr. at Washington, Avery Johnson at Kansas State, Camp at Duquesne and Fifita at Arizona, which is set to visit Pullman for a primetime matchup on CBS this Saturday.

At defensive line, where Hutson has started each of the Cougars’ first three games, the quarterback represents the goal he’s trying to reach. By now, Hutson knows the drill – he’s playing his fifth season at his fourth school, looking to hit the double-digit mark in career sacks – but he likes to envision the specific quarterback his team will be facing every week, the jersey he’ll be wearing, exactly what he looks like.

So after each of WSU’s first three games of the season, Hutson – “P3” to all his teammates and coaches – has picked up his phone and completed the same routine, the same as his goal on the field. He finds a photo of the quarterback of the upcoming opponent, saves it to his phone, then makes it his wallpaper, subbing out a photo of the quarterback the Cougars just played.

“I’m just a visual learner, visual memory guy,” Hutson said. “So everything I see, if I write it, I see it. If I look at it, I see it, and I just always can remember, ‘Hey, let’s get back to the center and remember what the goal is.’ So that’s just something that helps me personally just know what my goals are whenever things might be up or down, you know?”

“That sounds right,” WSU coach Kirby Moore added. “Paul is locked in every week to the objective on hand, and he has a great amount of energy every practice. He loves playing the game of football, and I think that’s contagious to his teammates as well.”

So far, Hutson has collected four total tackles on the season, three of the solo variety. Those may not sound like convincing numbers, but the job of an interior defensive lineman is often thankless, so consider this: Hutson has earned a Pro Football Focus defensive grade of 71.1, which ranks second on the team among players with 80 snaps. He’s also posted a run defense grade of 78.7, tops on the team using the same criteria.

In other words, Hutson is making an impact that’s equal parts invaluable and invisible. He’s anchoring a WSU defensive line that has looked like one of the team’s best position groups, on either side of the ball. And he’s doing it all slightly undersized, listed at 6-foot-1 and 270 pounds.

“My three game experience here has been great,” Hutson said. “Definitely for a senior season, it’s been everything I’ve imagined – playing in those big atmospheres, those big-time games is the reason I came here. I feel like just being able to play in those games has been really fun, and just experiencing it with the guys, to see how hard we worked all summer and just everything come together and us growing each and every week, to see us grow from week one to week three has been great.”

To get here, Hutson has had to follow a winding path. As a three-star prospect in the class of 2022, Hutson figured he would land at a power-conference school right out of IMG Academy, widely regarded as one of the country’s top talent hubs. Instead, Hutson took his talents to FCS Campbell, then transferred to Austin Peay, only to redshirt in 2023. Then in 2024, he returned to Campbell, which he parlayed into a spot at Marshall.

When last winter arrived, Hutson was on the move again. But this time, he was looking for something different, knowing this season would be his last. He wanted something meaningful, something family-oriented, something that would allow him to play his final year feeling satisfied with the way his career had unfolded.

So he got in touch with a longtime friend.

“Yo, bro, what’s up?” Hutson texted WSU defensive tackle Kaden Beatty. “What you trying to do?”

Turns out, Hutson and Beatty go way back, all the way back to playing Pop Warner in eastern Virginia where they grew up. They played on the same teams, in the same camps. They would get done with a long day of school or practice, then head back to Beatty’s place, where they would jump on the trampoline or play Madden, which Hutson says he’s always been better at than Beatty .

This winter, though, Beatty was ready to reunite with his Virginia buddy. He helped get Hutson’s film in front of Cougar coaches, Hutson said, which put the wheels in motion. Moore took Beatty’s word into consideration, he said, and besides, the Cougars wanted to find players with proven production on the field. Hutson checked all those boxes.

“It’s just great to see how far we’ve grown, both as players and just as men,” Hutson said. “It’s great to finish my last year and be able to play with him, alongside with him, train with him, work with him, and just achieve all our goals together.”

Still, to hear Hutson tell it, he hasn’t always felt so at home. It’s taken a toll on him, moving from city to city, school to school, quite literally every year of his life for the past four years. He’s always harbored confidence internally, he says, but showing it outwardly has required another level of conviction that he didn’t always have.

For example, he says, it took him some time to crawl out of his shell. “You’re always the new person,” Hutson said. Besides, back when he was a freshman at Campbell, Hutson was learning the value of humility at the same time. When he was coming out of IMG Academy, he envisioned himself going to a power conference school right away, the way alumni like Francis Mauigoa, Kaytron Allen and Carnell Tate did.

But Hutson landed at Campbell, an FCS program that didn’t play its first season of football until 2008. Then he went to Austin Peay, another FCS club with an all-time winning percentage of just 37%. “I went to the number one school in the country,” Hutson said, referring to IMG Academy, “and going to an FCS school was a humbling experience for me.”

“So I feel like that was the best opportunity for me to grow at that time in my journey,” Hutson added, “was to be humble and learn like, hey, continue to work, because when your time is called, it’ll be called.”

At Marshall, Hutson says, he finally got the kinds of opportunities he always imagined for himself. Playing in all 12 games, he made 40 tackles, including 6 ½ for loss and 3 ½ sacks. He also reeled in two interceptions. He also posted 21 pressures, which ranked in the top 30 in the Sun Belt that season.

“You’re on the stage. You’re able to fully put your talents on display,” Hutson said. “I feel like that was part of my journey as well of being able to show just my talents and everything I’ve done over the years, and have it on that stage.”

All of which seems to lead to this question: Is Hutson happy with the odyssey his career has turned into? He’s lived in six different states: Virginia, Florida, North Carolina, West Virginia, Tennessee and now Washington. He’s gone to one school, left for a season and returned the next. He says it’s helped him adapt, helped him feel comfortable in just about any situation he finds himself in.

But in Hutson’s eyes, how has his career lived up to the vision he saw for himself at the beginning? He doesn’t regret anything, he says, and he believes he’s taken a little something from each stop and applied it to his life as a whole. Now in his final year, he has arrived at the type of place he always visualized for himself.

He’s found he’s quite skilled at that kind of thing.

“As it stands right now, I’m definitely happy and I know that the younger version of myself would be very proud,” Hutson said. “Just knowing that I’ve done a lot of things that I’ve always put my mind out to, and I’ve set out to play at the highest level of football, make big plays in big-time games. The multitude of tackles and sacks and touchdowns, all those things. Just being able to have those things in my college career, I can say that I would definitely look back and be proud in knowing that it all came from the work that I invested in at a young age and just continued to hone in on and only get better at. So yeah, I would definitely say that at this moment, I’m proud for sure.”

Washington State.title: Oregon handles USC and the muddled future of matchups like Arizona-WSU | Week 4 picks
Washington State.summary:
Welcome the Hotline’s weekly picks against the point spread, published Thursdays throughout the regular season with a focus on the most intriguing matchups across the West and the top games nationally. Betting lines are courtesy of VegasInsider.com unless noted otherwise. (Games involving FCS teams not included.) I went 6-5-1 last week and am 15-20-1 for the season. Picks are for entertainment purposes only … unless they aren’t.

Oregon’s hotly anticipated duel with USC is one of two matchups of former Pac-12 teams Saturday in the late-afternoon TV window. The other will unfold 1,100 miles away on the Palouse, where Arizona visits Washington State in the first game of a home-and-home series.

The feline affair serves multiple purposes, allowing the Cougars to host a power conference opponent familiar to their fans and offering the Wildcats the chance to satisfy a Big 12 scheduling requirement.

The conference’s media rights agreement with ESPN and Fox stipulates that each team must play 10 games annually against Power Four opponents: nine in conference, one out of conference.

Because Arizona and WSU agreed to their series before the former officially left the Pac-12 for the Big 12 in August 2024, the Cougars qualify as a Power Four opponent. (The same standard applies to Oregon State, which faced Texas Tech and Houston earlier this season.)

But like so much else about the sport, the future of scheduling agreements between former Pac-12 schools now in different leagues is uncertain.

UCLA is under contract to play Cal for the rest of the decade and has a game with Utah in four years.

Arizona State has a two-year series with Stanford scheduled for the early 2030s.

And two ancient Northwest rivalries, the Apple Cup and Civil War, are in various stages of existence.

But that’s the extent of the nonconference inventory matching former Pac-12 teams, according to the website FBschedules.com, which tracks nonconferences series across the FBS and FCS.

A slew of games that seemingly make sense due to shared histories, geographic proximity and the location of alumni bases are not, at this point, lining future schedules of former Pac-12 peers.

Hopefully, that will change if the College Football Playoff takes the necessary steps to ensure quality nonconference inventory throughout the Power Four leagues.

The field is expected to double in size to 24 teams as early as next season. With that, the ACC, Big 12, Big Ten and SEC could implement standards designed to incentivize teams to craft rigorous nonconference schedules in much the same fashion the NCAA Tournament selection process rewards teams for high-level (e.g., Quadrant I) games outside of league play.

That could be problematic for Washington State, Oregon State and other schools in the rebuilt Pac-12. They would effectively be cast into purgatory as high-risk opponents (threats to win the game) that do not satisfy CFP scheduling requirements.

But for the 10 former Pac-12 schools now scattered across the ACC, Big 12 and Big Ten, a barrage of home-and-home series sprouting up in the late 2020s and early 2030s could prove beneficial.

There’s a fascinating alternative, too: NIL-driven matchups at neutral sites that mirror the multiteam events so popular in college basketball in November and December.

Why not match UCLA against Arizona State or Utah against Washington in Las Vegas – even better: make it a double-header – with sponsorship revenue going to each team’s NIL efforts?

A version of that model was put to use a few weeks ago, in fact.

Auburn was supposed to host Baylor but moved the game to Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, allowing the Peach Bowl “to provide opportunities for promotional appearances for Auburn players promoting ticket sales and ancillary events,” according to ESPN’s report last year.

Admittedly, there are a barrage of hurdles. The game(s) would need a sponsor to offer the name, image and likeness opportunities. The schools would need availability within schedules that have limited flexibility. And the coaches would need a competitive reason to follow the more challenging path.

As with most other aspects of college football, it’s largely about willpower – about the schools committing to solutions that serve both their fans and the game writ large. College football is best when doubling down on regional roots, on historic connections. But the decision-makers must have a clearly defined incentive structure.

We aren’t confident. By the early 2030s, nonconference matchups between former Pac-12 schools could go the way of the Dodo.

If the CFP does the right thing once expansion becomes official, then perhaps the schools will embrace an opportunity to elevate the sport across the region.

To the Week 4 picks …

(All times Pacific)Kickoff: Friday at 7:30 p.m. on ESPN

Comment: Absolutely nothing screams ACC football quite like Clemson playing in Berkeley on a Friday night at 10:30 p.m. Eastern … and the Bears rolling to a decisive victory. Pick: Cal

San Diego State (+3) at Toledo

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on CBS Sports Network

Comment: Combine the long trip with the early kickoff and a quality opponent – not to mention SDSU’s woeful aerial game – and this has the ingredients for an intra-Group of Six wipeout. Pick: Toledo

UCLA (-11/2

) at Maryland

Kickoff: 10:30 a.m. on Big Ten Network

Comment: The Hotline doesn’t plan to begin taking the Terps seriously if they win. But we definitely will stop taking the Bruins seriously if they lose. Pick: UCLA

Boise State (-7) at Western Michigan

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on ESPN2

Comment: Massive game in the Group of Six, with the winner assuming the pole position in the chase for the CFP automatic bid. Both teams struggled last week against inferior opponents: WMU edged Rice while Boise State had to beat back South Dakota. We suspect both had one eye on this showdown. Pick: Western Michigan

Iowa (+51/2

) at Michigan

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on CBS

Comment: First team to 14 wins. And covers. Pick: Iowa

Utah (-8) at Iowa State

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on Fox

Comment: Utah’s high-powered offense (47.3 points per game) hits the road for the first time and will encounter a well-drilled defense that should frustrate the Utes for two or three quarters before Byrd Ficklin blows the game open. Pick: Utah

Oklahoma State (+11/2

) at West Virginia

Kickoff: 4 p.m. on FS1

Comment: How will West Virginia handle the afterglow from its upset of Virginia? Our hunch: Not well enough to suit coach Rich Rodriguez. The winner should be taken seriously as a Big 12 contender. Pick: Oklahoma State

Oregon (-3) at USC

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on NBC

Comment: The most significant regular-season West Coast matchup since Oregon and Washington tangled in the last year of the old Pac-12. The stakes are particularly high for USC coach Lincoln Riley’s job security, and for Oregon’s playoff prospects. We aren’t convinced the Trojans have improved enough on defense to finally slay their nemesis. Pick: Oregon

Texas A&M (+81/2

) at LSU

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on ABC

Comment: With both teams coming off losses, this effectively stands as a playoff-elimination game – and the sport is better for it. With a 24-team CFP, the drama would be cut in half. Pick: LSU

Arizona (-10) at Washington State

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on CBS

Comment: The line initially felt a bit high. But the more we drilled into WSU’s offensive offense, the easier it became to justify a double-digit spread. The Cougars have scored 17 points in two games against Power Four teams (Washington and Kansas State) that are comparable in personnel to the Wildcats. Pick: Arizona

Missouri (+6) at Mississippi State

Kickoff: 4:45 p.m. on SEC Network

Comment: If you haven’t seen MSU’s Kamario Taylor, this is a good opportunity to watch one of the most gifted quarterbacks in the country. And for that reason, the Bulldogs are the sleepiest of sleepers to make the playoff. Pick: Mississippi State

Oregon State (-101/2

) at UTEP

Kickoff: 6 p.m. on MW+

Comment: The Beavers are trending toward an upside surprise this season with transfer quarterback Braden Atkinson. The Miners are the Miners. Tough to envision anything other than a comfortable win for the visitors. Pick: Oregon State

Georgia Tech (-3) at Stanford

Kickoff: 7:30 p.m. on ESPN

Comment: This is Stanford’s best chance all season for a conference victory – the Yellow Jackets are struggling on offense and extremely vulnerable – but the total of 47.5 is more enticing than the spread. And in case there was any question, we like the Under. Pick: Stanford

Minnesota (+91/2

) at Washington

Kickoff: 8 p.m. on Fox

Comment: Despite their well-documented struggles in Weeks 1 and 2, the Huskies should handle Minnesota with relative ease. If they don’t, well, it might be time for a red alert in Seattle. Pick: Washington

Straight-up winners: Cal, Toledo, UCLA, Boise State, Michigan, Utah, Oklahoma State, LSU, Oregon, Arizona, Mississippi State, Oregon State, Stanford and Washington

Five-star special: Mississippi State. The Bulldogs have been ultra-impressive thus far. The Tigers struggled to put away Troy last week.

Washington State.title: WSU QB Caden Pinnick is one of the country's best play-action passers. Could the Cougars incorporate more of that?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – DJ Warner is open about the part of his game that needs the most work. In his debut season at Washington State, he’s playing linebacker for the first time, and on several occasions, he’s admitted he wants to improve his pass coverage.

“The space is definitely the biggest difference,” said Warner, who played defensive end in his first two seasons of college ball. “I don’t have to take on every lineman with every pound in my body.”

As he learns to operate in space, he’s facing a tall task in defending WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick, who didn’t just lead the Cougars to their first win of the season with a blowout win over FCS Duquesne last weekend. Thanks in large part to a sharp second half, Pinnick now ranks No. 2 in the country in Pro Football Focus’ play-action passing grades, earning a grade of 94.4. He’s thrown two touchdowns on those kinds of plays, too.

In other words, only one quarterback in the entire country has been better than Pinnick on play-action throws, at least according to PFF’s assessments. The numbers back it up. He’s completed about 78% of his play-action passes, which ranks No. 20 nationwide, including No. 1 in the Pac-12. If you narrow it down to adjusted completion percentage – which removes plays outside of the quarterback’s control, like drops and throwaways – he’s checked in with a mark of 94.1%, which is No. 4 in the country.

That’s a nerdy way of expressing what has become clear in WSU’s first three games of the season: Pinnick is at his best rolling out of the pocket, when he has time to step into the throw and get some power behind his toss. He’s shown it in all three games thus far, in losses to Washington and Kansas State and a home win over Duquesne.

So how has Pinnick become so proficient at that part of his game? For one, it helps that he’s had time to throw, which has not always been the case on standard dropbacks. He was pressured 21 times against UW and 28 times against K-State, the latter of which was the second-best mark in the country for that week. The Cougars’ offensive line, which has since shuffled personnel, couldn’t buy him enough time on regular dropbacks.

So credit WSU coach Kirby Moore and offensive coordinator Matt Miller for identifying this part of Pinnick’s game: He’s best with some movement. That’s especially true when the Cougars’ ground attack is generating enough production to make defenses think twice on handoffs. Thing is, that wasn’t exactly happening against the Huskies and the Wildcats, which makes Pinnick’s play-action efficiency even more impressive.

“It starts with protecting the quarterback,” Moore said. “When we protect the quarterback, whether it’s drop-back, whether it’s play-action, whether it’s moving the pocket, and he trusts his eyes. He’s done a really nice job, and we gotta continue to improve that. You saw it there in the second half (against Duquesne), but it’s gotta show up consistently.”

Let’s break things down game by game. Against Washington on Sept. 6, Pinnick completed 9 of 10 play-action throws for 103 yards, a remarkable string of efficiency. In that game, the Cougars’ running backs combined for just 38 yards, which isn’t exactly enough to keep defenses honest. But Pinnick was good enough to overcome that.

On his first completion of the Apple Cup, Pinnick faked a handoff to running back Maxwell Woods and rolled out to his right, where he spotted receiver Daniel Blood, who hauled in the ball in stride. That catch, contested at that, moved the chains for the Cougars.

Later in the first quarter in that game, Pinnick faked a handoff to running back Kirby Vorhees, found receiver Darrius Clemons, stepped into the throw and laced a bullet downfield, good for another first down. Look at the coverage Pinnick sees on that play: With the UW linebackers out of the picture, caught out of position by the fake handoff, Pinnick had clearer lines of sight and took advantage.

Pinnick’s third play-action pass completion is even more impressive. He may have faked out a couple of UW defenders, but it didn’t work, at least not right away. He scrambled to his right, looking for an open receiver, then finally spotted Blood for a first down. Another play where Pinnick makes a strong throw on the run.

Pinnick showed off his proficiency in the play-action game twice more against the Huskies. The first of these two plays, simplified by Miller, only asked Pinnick to fake a handoff and find tight end Beau Baker open in the flat. He cashed in easily.

This next play bears a stark resemblance to the second one mentioned above. After faking a handoff, he had time to step into his throw, even with the Huskies’ linebackers dropping back into coverage, unfazed by the fake. With that time, Pinnick fired a line drive to Clemons, who has been sharp making contested catches in three games this fall.

“His play-action passes are amazing because that’s a part of my game that I need to work on on the defensive side of the ball,” Warner said. “So him attacking us in that game, him being able to take shots in the play-action pass and still have his threat on his feet has been big in practice.”

Let’s fast-forward to the following weekend, in WSU’s road loss to Kansas State. Pinnick wasn’t as clean in the play-action department in this game, completing just 2 of 5 attempts for 24 yards on those plays, but his two completions back up the conclusions we’ve been able to come to so far.

On one completion, he faked a handoff to Vorhees, which forced two K-State linebackers to race to the left side of the field. Pinnick took off to the right, and on the move, he found Clemons near the sideline. That pass covered 12 yards and gave the Cougs a first down.

On this front, Pinnick was at his very best against Duquesne, a winless FCS team that entered allowing north of 500 yards per game. In that way, Pinnick and the Cougars should have expected to deal damage to the Dukes’ defense. These next observations hardly come with an asterisk – they support the pattern that has become clear by now – but keep in mind the talent gap that the teams are operating with.

Still, Pinnick looked great. In his first play-action completion, he had time to set his feet and find Clemons, who has become one of Pinnick’s favorite targets on these kinds of plays. The play covered some 12 yards.

In this game, Moore gave some input in the playcalling game to Miller, so it’s hard to say who should get the credit for this next play. But whoever’s idea it was, it worked like a charm, springing tight end Jack Pedersen open over the middle for a touchdown. The play action sent two Duquesne linebackers to the right, Pedersen crossed to the left and before he knew it, he was jogging untouched into the end zone.

For our final play, we’re going to the end of Saturday’s third quarter, when the Cougars’ offense had finally woken up. To cash in for the second of three straight scoring drives, Pinnick faked a handoff, drifted to his right and found receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, who showed some real concentration to haul it in over a contest in the back of the end zone.

Here’s one more stat to wrap things up: Pinnick is running play-action on just 26% of his dropbacks, and among the top 10 quarterbacks in PFF’s play-action grades, Pinnick ranks second-to-last in play-action percentage. Could there be room in Miller and Moore’s playsheet for more play-action passes against Arizona this week?

If so, the Cougars might have a better chance of pulling an upset and heading into Pac-12 play with a strong dose of momentum.

“When we’re at our best, we’re running the ball, and our play-action is working well,” WSU left tackle Ashton Tripp said. “So when he’s able to throw the ball, I think we’re playing at our best.”

Washington State.title: After impressive day for WSU with old conference foe Arizona looming | Pac-12 power rankings
Washington State.summary:
The Pac-12 football power rankings are published each Sunday on the Hotline and consider both the latest results and season-long performance. Call it an objectively subjective look at the state of the conference. If you’re unhappy with the rankings, email us at the address below … or play better. For comparative purposes, we have included the placement of each team in last week’s rankings.

It looked bleak for the Pac-12 at roughly 9 p.m. Saturday night. No, not bleak. Gruesome. San Diego State was careening toward what would be a double-digit home loss to James Madison. Fresno State was locked in a field goal fest with San Jose State, and Boise State, a 28-point favorite, was in danger of an unimaginable loss to South Dakota.

Eventually, the conference escaped an #AfterDark disaster.

The Bulldogs pulled away from SJSU, and the Broncos made enough plays down the stretch to beat back their pesky foe.

Combine those victories with impressive displays by Washington State and Oregon State, which hammered FCS opponents, plus Texas State’s wild win over North Texas, and the Pac-12 emerged from Week 3 without major damage.

Up next: The defining Saturday of the season for the rebuilt conference.

Week 4 features just one matchup with a Power Four team – Washington State hosts Arizona in a Pac-12 legacy affair – but that’s exactly why the stakes are high on Sept. 26, the final weekend of inter-league play.

The Pac-12 has six dates with its peers in the Group of Six, offering an opportunity show it stands as the best league outside the Power Four:

• Two dates with the Mid-American, both on the road: Boise State visits Western Michigan, which lost in controversial fashion at Michigan two weeks ago, while San Diego State takes its struggling offense to Toledo.

• Two dates with the American: Fresno State hosts Rice, and Colorado State visits UTSA, which already owns one victory over the Pac-12 (a five-point win at Texas State).

• One date with the Mountain West: Oregon State and its dynamic offense visit floundering UTEP.

• One date with the Sun Belt: Utah State welcomes Troy, which lost by a mere 10 points at Missouri on Saturday.

Six defining games, four on the road and four against teams that could contend for their conference championships.

Boise State’s trip to WMU is the headliner, Broncos against Broncos with the winner taking pole position in the race for the Group of Six berth in the College Football Playoff.

But the other five will shape conference reputations and add valuable data to the strength-of-schedule and strength-of-record metrics at the heart of the CFP selection process.

By the close of business Saturday night, the rebuilt Pac-12 will know precisely where it stands in the hierarchy and whether the road to the playoff is narrow or wide.

To the power rankings …

1. Boise State (2-1)

Result: beat South Dakota 38-24

Next up: at Western Michigan

Comment: Looking back, the Hotline should have seen the South Dakota trap slotted into Boise State’s schedule after Memphis and before Western Michigan – two important Group of Six duels. The Broncos dominated with 533 total yards but made just enough mistakes, including a muffed punt return in the fourth quarter, to create the unexpected drama. (Last week: 1)

2. Oregon State (1-2)

Result: beat Montana 52-17

Next up: at UTEP (6 p.m. on MW+)

Comment: We aren’t saying the Beavers will earn a berth in the Pac-12 championship game, but we aren’t saying they won’t. At least, the Hotline isn’t prepared to rule them out just yet. The start under new coach JaMarcus Shephard has been undeniably impressive. (Last week: 2)

3. Fresno State (2-1)

Result: won at San Jose State 26-10

Next up: vs Rice (7 p.m. on The CW)

Comment: From here, it’s increasingly clear that tiers are forming. Boise State, Oregon State and Fresno State are on the highest, with a clear gap to the next level. Sure, that dynamic could change three times over before the season concludes. But there’s no fun in waiting for results before leaping to conclusions. (Last week: 4)

4. San Diego State (1-2)

Result: lost to James Madison 26-13

Next up: at Toledo (9 a.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: With 25 percent of the season complete, there is zero indication that quarterback Jayden Denegal has made the leap in efficiency SDSU requires in order to contend for the Pac-12 title. His completion percentage is 53.7, and the task doesn’t get easier this week. (Last week: 3)

5. Colorado State (2-1)

Result: lost to BYU 41-23

Next up: at UTSA (9 a.m. on ESPNU)

Comment: The Rams simply lacked the personnel to compete with BYU on the lines of scrimmage and were no match for bruising tailback LJ Martin (176 yards). But Boise State is the only team in the Pac-12 that approaches the Cougars’ physicality. We continue to expect CSU to be competitive on a regular basis. (Last week: 5)

6. Texas State (1-2)

Result: beat North Texas 49-35

Next up: vs. Incarnate Word (3 p.m. on USA Network)

Comment: No way to overstate the significance of Texas State’s win on team psychology, bowl math and Pac-12 narrative. North Texas was one week removed from blasting UNLV, purportedly one of the top teams in the Mountain West. And the Bobcats were fresh off a gut-punch loss to UTSA. (Last week: 7)

7. Washington State (1-2)

Result: beat Duquesne 48-7

Next up: vs. Arizona (4:30 p.m. on CBS)

Comment: Don’t interpret the result as proof the Cougars have fixed their anemic offense. After all, Duquesne lost to Youngstown State 70-13 two Saturdays ago. That said, scoring 48 points and gaining 512 yards is better than not doing either. (Last week: 6)

8. Utah State (0-3)

Result: lost at Utah 33-0

Next up: vs Troy (4:30 p.m. on CBS Sports Network)

Comment: Based on how the Aggies have performed and the breakdown of their conference schedule, we are beginning to think 0-12 is a distinct possibility. Much depends on the result this week. (Last week: 8)

Washington State.title: WSU to stick with new offensive line group, CB Jalil Tucker injury update and other notes
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Headed into a home showdown against Arizona this weekend, Washington State may have found an offensive line group that works best.

The Cougars are planning to stick with the same group that started last weekend against Duquesne, coach Kirby Moore said Monday: left tackle Ashton Tripp, left guard Jonny Lester, center Noah Dunham, right guard Nick Bakken and right tackle Jaylin Caldwell.

For WSU, that represents a change from the previous two games. In road losses to Washington and Kansas State, the Cougars started redshirt junior Kyle Martin at left guard and Lester at right tackle, where he had never started before. But against Duquesne, coaches benched Martin, moved Lester to left guard and slotted in Caldwell at right tackle, which paved the way for WSU to total 316 rushing yards, the program’s most in two decades, and that group didn’t allow a sack on quarterback Caden Pinnick.

That looked like WSU’s best five-man group yet this season, and the numbers back it up. In Saturday’s game against Duquesne, that unit finished with a Pro Football Focus pass-blocking grade of 72.7, by far the team’s best in three games, as well as a run-blocking grade of 72.1, also its best thus far.

Individually, both Caldwell and Lester earned pass-blocking grades north of 80. Caldwell finished at 86.3 while Lester checked in at 83.3. For Lester, it was another sharp game playing left guard, which is where he’s played some of his best games. Last season, when he had to play right tackle due to injuries, three of his four worst games came in those situations.

Additionally, all five offensive linemen on Saturday posted run-blocking grades north of 69, which is above average. That lines up with the explosive day the Cougars enjoyed on the ground, getting two 100-yard rushers in one game for the first time since 2005.

Moore also added that “we’re gonna need all six of those guys to keep each other fresh throughout the season,” referencing Martin, who has the lowest offensive PFF grade on the team at 28.1 as well as a pass-blocking grade of 0.0.

In other news, Moore seemed to express confidence in placekicker Jack Stevens, who has opened the season 1-for-5 on field goals, including a miss from 30 yards on Saturday. He also missed an extra point for the first time in his career

Asked Monday about the possibility of replacing him, Moore seemed to indicate the Cougars would stick with Stevens.

“We’re gonna go back to work. I think that’s the most important thing for us,” Moore said. “Operation, there’s been snap issues. There’s been protection issues. Obviously, we missed one there on Saturday. Jack’s made a ton of kicks throughout the offseason. Looking forward to seeing him make a bunch of kicks this week in practice and building up to Saturday.”

If WSU were to make a change, it would likely be to transfer kicker Miguel Arenas, who has spearheaded kickoff duties this fall. He seems to have the bigger leg between the two.

Also on Monday, Moore called cornerback Jalil Tucker’s status “day-to-day” with an injury he sustained in the Apple Cup on Sept. 6. A transfer from Oregon State, Tucker missed the next game against Kansas State, wearing street clothes on the sideline. Tucker dressed and warmed up for Saturday’s game against Duquesne, but didn’t play.

“Just made the decision there close to game time that he wasn’t gonna go,” Moore said. “We gotta see where he’s at here this week and anticipate being close to game time there on Saturday.”

In Tucker’s absence, WSU has tried a couple different approaches. Against K-State, the Cougars went with redshirt senior Kai Rapolla, who had a forgettable game, missing two tackles and allowing three catches on four targets. Against Duquesne, they moved nickelback Jamarey Smith to cornerback and brought safety Jackquintin Ball off the bench, which seemed to work better for the Cougars.

If Tucker can’t play against Arizona, look for coaches to go with the latter strategy once again.

Washington State.title: WSU set to host Arizona in matchup of legacy Pac-12 schools | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s home game against Arizona on Saturday afternoon.

What is it?

Fresh off registering his first win as WSU’s head coach with a rout over FCS Duquesne, Kirby Moore leads his club into a primetime matchup against legacy Pac-12 foe Arizona, which has opened the season 2-1. The Wildcats received 12 points in the latest AP Top 25 poll, good for an unofficial No. 36 ranking.

This game was scheduled back in January 2025, when WSU and Arizona agreed to a home-and-home series. The game in Tucson is set for next September.

It’s the teams’ first meeting since 2023, when the Wildcats stunned the Cougars with a 44-6 win in Pullman. Dating back to 2015, the Cougars won five of the past seven meetings.

Where is it?

Gesa Field at Martin Stadium in Pullman.

When is it?

Kickoff is set for 4:30 p.m.

Where can I watch it?

CBS will broadcast the game.

Who is favored?

As of Monday afternoon, WSU was around a 10.5-point underdog in most sportsbooks (fixed from earlier).

How did the Cougars fare last week?

WSU looked a bit sluggish in the first half against FCS Duquesne over the weekend, but thanks to an offensive explosion in the second, the Cougars pulled away with a 48-7 win, their first of the season. In the second half, the hosts scored on back-to-back punt returns , the first from safety Jaylen Thomas and the second from receiver Tank Hawkins, which was the program’s first time with two in one game since 1973.

WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick completed 17 of 22 passes for 196 yards, two touchdowns and one interception for the Cougars, who used a 34-0 second half to put a forgettable first half in the rearview mirror and pull away for good. The hosts also rushed for 316 yards, the program’s most since 2006, getting two 100-yard rushers: Maxwell Woods tallied 116 yards on 11 carries and Kirby Vorhees piled 109 yards on 9 carries.

“The good thing to see was more explosive plays. Rushed for 316 yards,” Moore said on Monday. “Kirby and Max both going for over 100 yards. Believe the first time in maybe 21 years here at Washington State. Thought Caden did a nice job distributing the football, also again being a playmaker on designed runs and scrambles, creating explosives there. Six-of-nine on third down, only faced two in the second half, which goes back to creating more explosives on first and second down.”

Moore was seen on the sideline carrying what looked like a playsheet, and after the game, Pinnick said his head coach had some input in the playcalling department. That helped the Cougars finally wake up on offense, as did the matchup against a winless FCS squad, which couldn’t stop the hosts from turning in an efficient 6-for-9 effort on third down – which had held WSU back in its first two losses of the season. Two Cougars, receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy and tight end Jack Pedersen, recorded their first regular-season touchdowns at WSU.

On defense, WSU held Duquesne to just 180 total yards, including just 75 through the air. Defensive end Matyus McLain and safety Jeremiah Bernard led the team with six sacks apiece, and the Cougs registered two sacks: One-half each from Bernard, defensive tackles Kaden Beatty and Damarjhe Lewis and linebacker DJ Warner.

But the Cougars ran into some problems on special teams, their two punt return touchdowns notwithstanding. In the second half, kicker Jack Stevens misfired on a 30-yard attempt from the left hash, making him 1-for-5 on field goals to open the season. He also missed an extra point for the first time in his career. Coaches stuck with him on extra points even after those two misses, but moving forward, keep an eye on whether that holds up or if coaches go to transfer kicker Miguel Arenas, who mans kickoff duties, for field goals as well.

On Monday, Moore was asked directly whether he would consider making a change at kicker.

“We’re gonna go back to work. I think that’s the most important thing for us,” Moore said. “Operation, there’s been snap issues. There’s been protection issues. Obviously, we missed one there on Saturday. Jack’s made a ton of kicks throughout the offseason. Looking forward to seeing him make a bunch of kicks this week in practice and building up to Saturday.”

Scouting Arizona …

The Wildcats, who are led by head coach Brent Brennan and quarterback Noah Fifita, have started the season with a win over FCS Northern Arizona, a road loss to ranked BYU and a home victory over Northern Illinois. They’re pushing for a spot in the AP Top 25 for the first time since the final week of last season.

Fifita, who was in the middle of a breakout year in 2023 when the Cougars last faced the Wildcats, is off to a torrid start to the season: He’s completed 81% of his passes for 834 yards, seven touchdowns and just one interception, earning him Big 12 Player of the Week honors. He’s flanked by top running back Kendrick Reescano, who has tallied 127 rushing yards and two scores on 33 carries, while two receivers have led the way for Arizona: Giovanni Richardson has 161 yards on 14 catches, and Tre Spivey has 149 yards and two scores on 12 receptions.

The Wildcats, who had to erase an early 10-0 deficit to blow out Northern Illinois over the weekend, lean on the pass more than the run. They rank near the bottom of the country in rushing attempts per game – they run the ball 43% of the time, which is No. 116 nationally – and their passing offense generates 281 yards per game, No. 34 in the country. Much of that is thanks to Fifita, who became Arizona’s all-time leader in passing yards in Saturday’s game against Northern Illinois.

“Very accurate passer, ton of completions, can extend plays. He’s a playmaker,” Moore said of Fifita. “We gotta play team defense. Trust your teammate that he’s doing his job. Sometimes you try and force something or you’re pressing, and he’s able to extend the play and then find guys downfield.”

A couple names to know on Arizona’s defense are linebacker Taye Brown and edge rusher Cooper Blomstrom, who have combined for two sacks on eight quarterback pressures this fall, making their matchup with the Cougars’ new-look offensive line one to watch.

What happened last time?

Back in 2023, Arizona walked into Gesa Field and blew WSU out to the tune of 44-6, a shocking result for a Cougar team that was ranked No. 19 at the time. After scoring an opening touchdown, the Cougs were outscored 44-0 the rest of the game.

That was WSU’s second loss in what turned into a six-game skid.

Washington State.title: WSU Football: Highlights vs. Duquesne | 9/19/26
5 thoughts from WSU's blowout win over Duquesne | Rewind
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – As Washington State marched closer and closer to this weekend’s game, which turned into a 48-7 rout over winless FCS squad Duquesne, the Cougars found themselves in a tricky spot.

If they completely dominated, they would do what they were expected to. If they didn’t, well, some of the concerns about coach Kirby Moore and offensive coordinator Matt Miller’s offense would grow even louder.

For WSU, it wasn’t exactly a lose-lose, but it was somewhere in the area.

In Saturday’s first half, the Cougars didn’t look sharp, taking only a 14-7 lead into halftime. In the second, quarterback Caden Pinnick and his unit roared to life, using a 34-0 half to run away with a convincing blowout. Considering the circumstances, it was just about exactly what WSU needed.

Here are five thoughts from the game and what it means for WSU moving forward.

1. WSU simplified some things on offense: Some of the bigger concerns from Washington State’s previous game, a lopsided road loss to Kansas State, centered around some of the opportunities the Cougars’ offense missed.

On two straight plays, a third-and-short followed by a fourth-and-short, WSU’s outside receiver sees a big cushion from his defender. In those spots, Pinnick could have checked into a play to hit that receiver for a quick pass and an easy first down. Instead, the Cougs stick with inside runs, both of which get turned away.

On Saturday against Duquesne, WSU saw the same look, and this time Pinnick took advantage. On one play in the second quarter, receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy gets a nice cushion of coverage, so he’s able to turn around for an easy pitch-and-catch. To convert a third down in the first frame, Ganashamoorthy sees another cushion, but he runs a clear-out route to make room for wideout Daniel Blood to make an easy catch. Then in the second quarter, Pinnick makes a similar connection with receiver Darrius Clemons.

That helped Pinnick finish with a Pro Football Focus passing grade of 90.7, the third-best mark in the country in Week 3 of college football, which is remarkable considering the fact he threw a bad interception on his first pass of the game. Chalk that up to Pinnick’s sharp response, completing 7 of 8 passes for 110 yards and two touchdowns in the second half.

2. Woods could be in for a big year: WSU turned in an impressive stat from Saturday’s game: Running backs Maxwell Woods and Kirby Vorhees each rushed for 100-plus yards, becoming the first Cougar duo to do so in one game since 2005. That was part of WSU’s 316-rushing yard day in total, the program’s most in one game since 2006.

That’s an extraordinary development, and it might give us a window into the vision Moore has for this offense. In Saturday’s game, he was seen on the sideline carrying what looked to be a play sheet, which he didn’t do in either of the Cougars’ first two games of the year. After the game, he called playcalling duties a “collaborative effort” alongside Miller, with Pinnick adding that Moore had some input.

So was the Cougars’ 48-point outburst a product of Moore’s involvement or the result of playing a bad FCS team? It’s hard to say, but it’s worth examining the way the Cougs involved Woods, perhaps the team’s fastest and shiftiest running back. He was the team’s leading rusher with 11 carries while Vorhees chipped in nine rushes.

If WSU wants to pull an upset and topple Arizona next weekend, Woods might find himself at the center of his team’s rushing attack. For evidence, look no further than the way the Cougs used Woods on a trick play, breaking him free for 45 yards on a direct snap.

3. The Cougars got creative to record two sacks, but should they have needed to? Defensive coordinator Trent Bray dialed up a few sharp blitzes, bringing safety Jeremiah Bernard into the fold for one and linebackers Isaiah Hung and DJ Warner in for another. Hung’s emergence is something to monitor – in the last two games he has played 41 and 39 snaps, respectively, pushing starter Keith Brown in that department – and Bernard’s athleticism and willingness to hit makes those ideas splendid.

But there’s another pattern developing: Edge rushers Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk, hailed as the WSU defense’s top two players, haven’t made huge splashes yet. In Saturday’s game, they combined for just three pressures. Against K-State, the number was just one, which came from McLain (who was courted strongly by the Wildcats over the offseason).

Those two see lots of double-teams, which is part of the reason why they haven’t been the wrecking balls they were projected to be headed into this season. But can they find a way to generate more pressure against Arizona? That’ll be a key storyline to keep an eye on.

4. WSU missed a real opportunity at the end of the first half: In fall camp, the Cougars spent oodles of time repping the exact situation that came up at the end of Saturday’s first half: clock under two minutes, ball in their own territory, looking to score before the end of the half. It was clear Moore placed a high priority on capitalizing in those kinds of scenarios.

So when the real thing came around against FCS Duquesne, why didn’t the Cougs give it a shot? They didn’t show any real urgency to move the ball down the field, running three inside runs for Vorhees to kick off the drive. They didn’t try their first pass until the clock ticked under 20 seconds.

At the time, it seemed like a signal from coaches on the way they viewed their offense, which later felt even stranger because of the way the Cougs erupted in the second half. In the end, it didn’t matter against an FCS team, but it very well could against a Power 4 opponent like Arizona.

“I need to look at that one more (time),” Moore said. “I do think there was a slippery, slow, fine line with that. We got the ball first to start the second half. I can’t remember the yardage on the first play, but I don’t think it was a second-and-2, and so if you go three-and-out quick there, you might give the ball back to them a little bit quicker than you want to. We have to look at that. I think we could have had a better plan just altogether in that situation.”

5. WSU’s new-look offensive line excelled: The Cougars rolled out a new lineup on their offensive line on Saturday, and it worked wonders: Left tackle Ashton Tripp, left guard Jonny Lester, center Noah Dunham, right guard Nick Bakken and right tackle Jaylin Caldwell didn’t give up a single sack, finishing with an over PFF pass-blocking grade of 72.7, their best mark of the season. Their run-blocking grade was 72.0, also their best figure yet.

To make that happen, coaches benched left guard Kyle Martin and moved Lester from right tackle to left guard, which is where he played his best games last season. Then they brought Caldwell in at right tackle, and he earned a PFF pass-blocking grade of 86.3, also his best grade of the season.

After the game, Moore wouldn’t commit to sticking with that lineup moving forward, but it appears to be the team’s best five-man group so far.

“I probably gotta look at the tape before I completely give you an answer on that,” Moore said. “Obviously, running for 316 yards there, there was some really good things that those guys did up front. There was definitely some lapses, whether it was protection, whether it was finishing there in the first half. So we’ll have to take a look at it. I know we’re gonna need all six of those guys.”
