Washington State.title: After blowout win over Duquesne, what’s the status of WSU’s special teams unit?
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Early in the week, when Washington State coach Kirby Moore was discussing a recent loss and looking ahead to his team’s next game, he considered how his guys could absorb the loss of receiver Tony Freeman.

Freeman is set to miss the rest of the season with an injury, so others would have to step up. What about speedy wideout Tank Hawkins? Could the Cougars find a spot for him?

“We have to,” Moore said.

What Moore probably couldn’t have predicted was the way Hawkins got involved. In the fourth quarter of WSU’s 48-7 win over Duquesne on Saturday afternoon, he took a punt back 65 yards for a touchdown, jetting around defenders on his way to the end zone. It amounted to a perfect use of Hawkins’ skillset.

Except that wasn’t the only damage the Cougars did on special teams in Saturday’s game. One punt return prior, safety Jaylen Thomas returned a punt 47 yards to the house. With back-to-back punt returns for touchdowns, WSU didn’t just register its first of those in a decade. The Cougars also turned in two punt return touchdowns for the first time since 1973.

“Jaylen Thomas, who’s done it on defense, doing it now on special teams. That guy’s special,” Moore said of Thomas, who also picked off two passes against Kansas State last weekend. “Tank Hawkins, really good to see him out in space.”

For WSU, the meaning here goes deeper than just two eye-popping punt returns. The Cougars needed those to resuscitate their special teams unit, which had turned in two forgettable showings to kick off the season, including in losses to Washington and Kansas State. Against UW, the Cougars botched two kick returns. Against K-State, the Cougars allowed a punt return of some 60 yards, which the Wildcats used to set up a short touchdown moments later.

So in that way, Thomas’ and Hawkins’ plays weren’t just fun sequences against an overmatched FCS club like Duquesne. They were also confidence-builders for coach Derek Sage, who mans the team’s special teams unit and wide receivers. No USA Network cameras panned to him in Saturday’s game, but it’s probably fair to say he wore a wide smile after those two returns.

Then there’s the matter of WSU’s placekicking. On Saturday, kicker Jack Stevens misfired on his only field goal attempt of the game, a 30-yard try from the left hash. That makes him 1-for-5 to open the season. He also missed an extra point, the first time he’s done so in his career. His only made field goal has come on a 42-yard connection against UW. Since then, he’s missed three straight field goals.

Earlier in the season, this pattern felt more uncharacteristic than anything. Stevens missed only three field goals last season, going 16-for-19 on the year, and in fall camp this year, he was consistently accurate. But now it’s turned into a significant problem for WSU, which might have to make a change at that position.

“I got a ton of confidence in Jack,” Moore said. “He’s done it throughout the offseason. We gotta look at the whole operation. There’s snap, there’s hold, there’s protection, there’s a lot of pieces to that. Obviously, we gotta improve, and we’re gonna do that.”

Where could the Cougars look? Their other kicker is North Texas transfer Miguel Arenas, who mans the team’s kickoff duties, likely because he has a bigger leg – just not the more accurate one. But now, as Stevens continues to miss the kinds of field goals that looked like chip shots for him last fall, Arenas could be in line for a bigger role.

It’s worth keeping in mind that even after Stevens missed his field goal, coaches kept him in for extra points. And even after he missed one of those, coaches stuck with him. That probably boosted his confidence.

But as WSU prepares for a home showdown with Arizona next week, a primetime tilt on CBS, the Cougars need their best pieces in place. On Saturday, they showed a willingness to make changes by benching left guard Kyle Martin. It’ll be interesting to see if Cougar coaches show the same kind of readiness to do to the same in their placekicking department.

Washington State.title: Cougar Men to Face Seattle U at Seattle Holiday Classic in December
WSU hoops to meet Seattle U at Seattle Holiday Classic in December
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Chalk up another game on Washington State’s nonconference hoops schedule.

The Cougars will meet Seattle University on Dec. 19 at the Seattle Holiday Classic, according to a Monday news release, set for Climate Pledge Arena. It’s part of a doubleheader showcase, which will also pit University of Washington against Baylor.

“We’re looking forward to getting back to Seattle and bringing Cougar basketball to the thousands of WSU alumni in western Washington,” WSU coach David Riley said in the release. “I believe playing the other Division-I teams in the state is an important part of developing the game and honoring its history in the Pacific Northwest. We look forward to facing the Redhawks at Climate Pledge Arena and welcoming Coug fans to the Seattle Holiday Classic.”

It’ll be the third meeting in the last two seasons for WSU and Seattle U, which split last season’s series, then a West Coast Conference matchup. The Redhawks earned a 69-55 win in Seattle, and the Cougars followed with a 70-58 victory about a month later in Pullman.

It also represents another chance for each head coach to match wits. Riley and Seattle U coach Chris Victor were both assistant coaches at Eastern Washington from 2015-17. In fact, both head coaches ran the same first play during their first matchup last season in Seattle.

“The same exact first set, a Spain action,” Riley said after that game. “Just totally random. I thought it was funny. We worked together for a couple years at Eastern. He’s a great person. Every once in awhile, you can have some fun in these games.”

WSU’s next roster includes 13 newcomers: Mohamed Sankhe (France), East Texas A&M transfer forward Ronnie Harrison, Northwestern transfer forward Tyler Kropp, Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell, Central Missouri (DII) transfer guard Lazerek Houston, TCU transfer guard RJ Jones, Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins, Sancho Moraga (Spain), Roman Stathis (Australia), Manhattan transfer forward Fraser Roxburgh, UNLV transfer forward Ladji Dembele, Eastern Washington transfer wing Casey Jones (who was previously on a two-year church mission), Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips and freshman forward Brayden Kyman.

Here is WSU’s known nonconference slate.

• At Washington (exh.), TBA.

• Vs. Davidson, TBA.

• Vs. Duke (Palm Springs), Nov. 21.

• Vs. Idaho, Nov. 27.

• At Murray State, Nov. 30.

• Vs. North Dakota State, Dec. 6.

• At Seattle U, Dec. 19

• Vs. EWU (Spokane), Dec. 22.

• At LSU, Dec. 28.
